Entertaining read that reminded me pleasantly of the BBC Sherlock special The Abominable Bride. 
 Pastiches are tricky business, which is why typically I abstain. I saw the author of this one speaking at a book festival and thought the themes she mentioned sounded interesting (Sherlock's artistry & vulnerability), and that she was genuinely fond of the character, so I decided to try this one. 
 Although the book makes the effort to present itself as an unpublished early case story of Dr. Watson's, it's closer in tone to the modern Sherlock interpretations than the canon stories - as you might expect from a volume that mentions the BBC actors by name in the acknowledgement. 
 On the one hand, I can see how this might ruffle some feathers. The writing style was a bit stiff at times, a little modern in others, and there was a sense of self reference to some pages that I could see breaking immersion for some people. 
 Personally, however, I like modern Sherlock so I enjoyed it. The focus on Sherlock's inner workings, Mycroft's prominence, and the prevalence of humor (particularly with Watson) are all big plusses for me, even if they do set the story apart from the original stories or more stringent pastiches. 
 If you're looking for strict adherence to canon in style, tone, and characterization maybe try Anthony Horowitz's House of Silk, which was endorsed by the Doyle estate. For everyone else, settle in to enjoy a fun read with strong characterization, vivid descriptions and action, and a solid adventure plot.

This book made me tear up in the middle and to be honest, I'm not even sure why. Maybe it was the feelings I had coming off of Torn Away. Maybe it was the fact that I was tired. I'm not sure guys. It wasn't even all that sad. 
 Rumble was the first Ellen Hopkins book I can say that I read and understood. I read Crank at one point, but I was kind of naive and didn't really understand that it was about crystal meth. (Let's be honest. I didn't even understand the verse poetry.) I now know that Hopkins writes about serious issues and in this particular novel, suicides and the repercussions it has on the people that are left to mourn. 
 I have a thing with liking books where the characters are questioning religion. I always find it kind of refreshing to read about for some reason. I really liked the essay bits that represented Matt's writing although I don't think a teacher would give him a good grade for what he wrote. The characters were mildly characterized. Hayden and Alexa were kind of flat but I thought that I could understand Matt's personality pretty well. 
 I did have a few problems with this one though. 
 I could not, for the life of me, ever connect with Hayden or Matt. I sympathized, but I never could really say that I connected with him. I though Hayden was sleazy throughout the whole novel. I'm not really sure if I like Matt or not. Sometimes I thought he was a new level of overly obsessive and at other times I just wanted to resurrect his dead brother for him. The love triangle was kind of annoying seeing as the development wasn't as great as I thought it would be. Hayden is kind of a terrible girlfriend and Matt is kind of a terrible boyfriend. At first, I didn't even understand why they were together because their relationship was all types of unhealthy. And Alexa is just a mess. I shipped Alexa and Matt but reading about the jealousy and drama between all of them wasn't that great. On top of it, I didn't like the development of the romance whatsoever. It felt kind of insta-love-y and I felt like it detracted from the bulk of the plot. 
 It also bugged me that Matt always said he loved Hayden but at the same time, kept thinking about Alexa. If that isn't a sign that something is wrong, I don't know what is. 
 The entire book I was waiting for what was referred to as "the rumble" (Which, for the record, doesn't show up until like page 350-60ish. Takes forever to build up to it and all the rising action is kind of boring). It wasn't really surprising and I was disappointed when I realized that that scene was the "big moment" that was supposed to be the turning point. It might have been an emotionally charged scene where Matt realizes that everything he's believed was wrong but I was expecting it to happen at some point. I just didn't expect it to be the climax of the novel. I know I probably sound a bit cray right now because you probably don't know what I'm talking about but I can't spoil. Sorry! 
 I enjoyed the writing. It was poetic but at the same time it also was pretty in a simple way. 
 I did like the ending, right before Matt gets into the hospital. I liked the shooting he did and I liked the way he grew from the experience. But I wish Hopkins had covered less in the novel. She tried to cover suicide, homosexuality, family problems, bad romantic relationships, etc, all in the same novel, and at times, I found it cumbersome. I think I would have enjoyed the novel more if it had focused on one specific topic. 
 3.5/5 Stars

I rarely find myself venturing into the world of magic realism because past experience has resulted in me finding it rather disengaging, a little silly, and frankly just not my taste. However, I was drawn in by the premise of this novel and hoped that it would mark a change for my relationship with the style. On this it has; I truly enjoyed this novel. The Strange and Beautiful Sorrows of Ava Lavender lives up to its name in many ways, being both strange and very beautiful. It is undeniably unique and was a reading experience like no other. 
 Ava Lavender tells this story like a multi-generational memoir in her own voice, making her the narrator and the ultimate centre of the story but drawing her mother, Viviane, and maternal grandmother, Emilienne, in as vivid and vital characters in their own right. Ava tells of each woman's life, focusing especially on each's loves and sorrows and the need for freedom from various traps and cages. Over the course of the narrative, all three women become more intriguing and more understandable, more familiar and yet also more mysterious. It is an excellent balance that suits the story so well. Each of the characters explored in the novel - not just these three central women - is undeniably strange in some way or another and has some kind of important effect on the lives of Emilienne, Viviane, and/or Ava. Watching this play out the way it does was truly engaging as they all struggle with what life throws their way. 
 Once again being true to its name, this novel has a strand of sorrow that weaves its way throughout the entire narrative. It displays itself more prominently in many ways (often related to love) but is clearly present during the whole story and adds a great deal to the feeling of the novel. The emotions that rise and fall in the telling of this story were one of the most powerful parts for me. I felt they were woven so well together and the memoir format helps bring them alive in the forefront. The love that comes and goes and the family bond that quietly permeates so many of the interactions feel so honest that I couldn't help but feel affected. 
 The magic realism was, to me, handled with a light hand and a subtle touch and I think that is why I enjoyed it significantly more than I often do. There were occasions where something especially peculiar pulled me out of the story a bit, but someone used to the quirks of magic realism I think would find this an enjoyable adventure throughout. 
 This novel really is so unique and immersive. The narrative is one that slowly pulls you deep into these characters' lives so you become invested almost without realizing, and yet also manages to maintain a distance that strikes a masterful balance. If you're looking for a sorrowful, beautifully written tale of human hearts and all the good and bad they take, this is the novel for you. If you're looking for YA with a very literary feel, this one is for you. Even if you're looking for a book set in the past that is not at all about the history, this book is for you. All these wonderful elements blend together so well to create this wonderful piece of literature. For a style that I do not often enjoy, this one truly took me by surprise.

Brutal. 
 This book in one word is Brutal with a capital B. I had started reading this book a few months back but within the first few pages I realized I wasn't in the mood for this kind of book. I am so very glad I came back to it when my mood changed. If you like war games set against a sci-fi/fantasy backdrop, with well-developed characters, and a compelling story of overcoming a corrupt political system then this book is written for you. 
 Red Rising is a story about a young man that lives a simple life of work and family and love. Darrow is talented; among the best at what he does despite his young age, so he has some standing among his tribe, but he is destined for a hard short life in a harsh unforgiving world full of rules and little rewards. But he has Eo, his equally young but wise beyond her years wife and the love he has for her gives him purpose. 
 And then she is taken from him in one of the cruelest ways I have ever read. This scene wrecked me. I can't even imagine having to be a participant in the death of a loved one.  So, understandably, he goes a little off the rails. He doesn't just want revenge against the man that took her away from him; he wants to bring down the whole damn system in blazing ball of fire and ash. And of course there are people ready and waiting to ignite that fire. 
 After Darrow finds out everything he has ever believed was a lie he allows himself to become a weapon for the cause. He has been hollowed out by the death of Eo, so it is easy for the Sons of Ares to fill him with the skills he will need to infiltrate the ranks of the elite that have enslaved them. He becomes a goddamn gladiator and marches willingly into the coliseum with the lions because to not live this lie to the fullest will mean failure to fulfill Eo's dream and avenge her death. 
 Just. So. Amazing. 
 There are so many things I enjoyed about this book... 
 First, the characters all have enormous depth. With the exception of maybe Darrow, but he lost his ability to depth the day he pulled his wife's legs to make her suffering less and now has a single-minded goal of destruction guiding his every decision. Although there was character development on his part, I needed him to remain the wrath of the movement to stay true to the character he became the day Eo died.  The women of this novel are strong. Like, really strong in terms of perseverance, intelligence, resourcefulness, and bravery (not to mention they are deadly as all hell). I would have liked to have seen what a house of only women warriors would have looked like to Pierce in this story. But that's almost the beauty of this world because among the elites, the women are just as formidable as the men and to underestimate them would mean your death. I get the sense they wouldn't have ever even considered a house of only male warriors superior to a house of only female warriors so we get equal opportunity murder and mayhem for this version of life on Mars. Darrow's lieutenants are fascinating; I love them all for different reasons. This book could have easily devolved into a mindless bloodbath, but there is so much STRATEGY and build throughout the book that I was completely pulled into the lives of these people. 
 There is Action! This book is not for the squeamish; there is blood, and lots of it. I have heard people compare this to The Hunger Games, and I sort of get it because there are 12 districts/12 houses and fights to the death among a group of teens in a "game" setting, but really that is where the comparison ends. I LOVED The Hunger Games, but I am also falling hard for Red Rising. 
 The world of Red Rising is interesting and unique. Caste systems are not a new concept, making other planets hospitable for human life is not a new concept, fighting against the system is NOT a new concept. Yet, Pierce Brown has managed to take all of these "not new" concepts and make them shiny and new and exciting all over again. There is some jargon used in the book that is a little hard to get through it at first (this is the reason I walked away from the books a few months ago and knew it was not what I needed right then) and there is significant world building that has to happen for the story make sense. It doesn't all get explained early on, but it is revealed to you as it is revealed to Darrow so there is a method to it and some of the dreaded info-dumping is there, but not as bad as it could be for a book like this. I think it was all written very well. 
 There is very little romance. Darrow's one true love's death is what sets this whole book in motion very early on in the story so despite there being temptation along the way, he doesn't acknowledge it, much. There is some "off screen" romance between a few secondary characters, but if you are looking for a break from insta-love, then this is going to be a perfect fit. 
 There were also some pieces that didn't quite fit for me... 
 They put so much effort into making Darrow perfect. Like painful surgery after surgery, body mods on top of layers of more body mods. His bones, his muscles, his eyes, his hair, his skin, you name it and it is scraped off and replaced (and it is described in painful detail). But, if perfection is the goal for the entire society of elite leaders (the Golds), why do not more of them do this? They feed him enhancers to increase the rate at which he can build muscle, and even increase his ability to retain force-fed intelligence. But why don't they all do it? 
 There were two other bits that annoyed me but they didn't ruin my enjoyment of the story and they are pretty big spoilers. DON"T CLICK THE SPOILER LINK if you don't want to know. I'm serious damn it, it could ruin the reading experience for you.  1) How could Dancer not know that Titus had made it into the school, and if he knew, why the hell didn't he tell Darrow? They could have been strong allies from the start and would have bettered their chances of success in the games. 2) How did none of the potential benefactors notice what was happening in the games with the proctors showing favor to the Jackal? It was clear that Darrow had won Priam for his house, but then was never served the honor because the proctors wouldn't allow it. I feel like they would have seen these games play out frequently enough before that they would recognize what was happening.   
 Overall, this book was everything I needed it to be when I needed it to be it. It may not be that for everyone who reads it, but do yourself a favor and wait until your mood is right before you pick it up because once you do, you won't be able to put it down. For me this is a 4.5 rounded up to a 5 because I was actually surprised at how much I liked it and only got one hour of sleep last night because I couldn't stop reading.

This book....this protagonist!!! 
 Kiera Cass has this ability at making me frustrated with her lead characters. Honestly at this point, it is a gift that she has. Because this Eadlyn Schreave is. AN. ANNOYING. LITTLE. BRAT! 
 I feel like whenever I make reviews about the books in this series I do them angrily but I swear I like it in a weird way. Although, I prefer America or as I call her 'Merica, one thousand times over Eadlyn. 
 The book is an easy read. The writing styles is easy to understand and fast to read. It is broken up nicely and makes the story completely clear to the reader. The main character is frustrating and annoying but I stuck with her because I felt she was going to grow and she did...a little bit. 
 In this review I am going to cover: 
 The Characters 
 What I liked 
 What I didn't like 
 What I think it's going to happen 
 The Characters 
 I am only going to focus on the three main guys that stood out to me which are: Kile, Henri, and Erik. 
 Eadlyn BRATT Schreave 
 This girl infuriates me!! From the very beginning of the book she says: "I am Eadlyn Schreave and no one is powerful as me" Once I read this, I wasn't put off, I just thought, "ok, it is hard being the future queen. Maybe she is just trying to stay strong" WRONG! This girl 100% believes this and becomes surprised when people don't think the same way. 
 She gets better because she genuinely thinks she is doing good and doesn't know any better. She is just stupid and very bad at making decisions, just like her mother. 
 Kile Woodwork 
 I love this guy! He is the only one (other than Ahren) that can but Eadlyn in her place! He is such a smart guy who has this sweet side to him that he is afraid to show. I love that he is the son of a character from the previous books. You really can see they resemble each other. 
 Henri....something. I can't remember it. 
 Oh sweet Henri! Being an English learner myself, I connected so much with Henri because at a certain point, I was just like him! He is such a goofball and lovable character. I just want to snuggle him and be like "good, good!" Although, I do know that the prospect of both of them ending together is slim...*sighs* 
 Erik...again I don't know. 
 When Erik first showed up, you thought he was just going to be part of the comic relief along with Henri...because you know...being the third wheel can be funny. However, as you continue, you get to know him and see how much of a hard worker he is. Additionally, you notice he is the type that is quiet but observes EVERYTHING. Nothing escapes this guy. So, you start to wonder if there is something developing between the two of them. It was such a nice surprise! He has got to be older, there is no way he is this mature by only being 18-19. 
 SPOILERS AHEAD 
 What I liked 
 I liked the mystery surrounding who she is going to choose or even if she IS going to choose anyone. In the Selection, you could immediately tell that America was going to end up with Maxon. However, here, we have so many good prospects. In a way, you go with her through the selection as you keep wondering which one of them is going to win her heart and our hearts along with them. Although I have to say Henri and Erik kinda won me over...but I still like Kile...AHH! I don't know! 
 I liked that we got to see the characters from the previous books quite often. It was fun to see them how they had grown up. I also liked that she showed just how much Maxon and America love each other still. SO cute! 
 Additionally, I liked that the whole caste dissolving thing wasn't a magical fix. It is the main cause of all the political problems in this book which made it feel more realistic. 
 What I didn't like 
 Ok, I am normally not picky but I have a list here. 
 I didn't like that Eadlyn was such a spoiled brat. I get she grew in the lap of luxury but come on, her mother was a five and her parents have worked so hard in making everyone equal! It felt a little bit unrealistic that she was such oblivious about everything and thought her subjects all 'loved her'. It is okay to be a little bratty and over confident but this was in a whole another level. We could have had the same development and arc if she had been tone down a little bit. 
 I didn't like that the America we see now is almost an entire new person. I get that she is older now and she had to become queen but c'mon! Get some of her bossy attitude in there! They only thing I saw from the old 'Merica was when she told Eadlyn "One, Watch your tone" That was it! 
 I also wished we saw more of the world she has built up through the books. We literally step outside the palace ONCE and it's for a parade. I wanted to see how everything looked over there! 
 Lastly, I wished there was more action, like in the other books. The only action we get is when the boys fight in the kitchen. 
 What I think is going to happen 
 I think that the monarchy is going to be dissolved or a plan will go in place to dissolve it. I don't think she is going to end up with a ring on her finger. I even suspect she not going to end up with anyone. I hope she does though! I don't think America is going to die...she better not! 
 All in all, this book is frustrating but you can't help but read it. Again is a weird thing with Kiera Cass' books. I hate it and I love it. LOL

Melanie lives in a cell. On weekdays, soldiers come into her cell with a wheelchair and strap her to it so that she can be taken to her classroom. She doesn't think they like her very much. She even jokes that she won't bite, which no one seems to find funny at all. In spite of it all, Melanie loves school and she's easily the smartest kid in the class. She doesn't realize it, but she exhibits a genius-level I.Q. 
 Sergeant Parks is one of the soldiers that comes to collect Melanie. He points the gun at her so that she won't bite his men as they strap her to her wheelchair. He knows Melanie isn't quite like the rest of the hungries, but it doesn't mean that he trusts her. 
 Helen Justineau is Melanie's favorite teacher. She's been a somewhat unwilling participant in this experiment with sentient hungries. Her job is on the line as she refuses to maintain a clinical level of distance from her classroom full of test subjects, particularly the sweet and brilliant Melanie. 
 Caroline Caldwell is the scientist in charge of studying this intriguing breed of hungries. Her goal is to figure out what it is that makes these young subjects different from the brainless cannibals that have wiped out most of civilization. If she can figure it out, she might be able to create a vaccination or even a cure. She has absolutely no qualms about cutting open the heads of her young specimens. After all, they're already dead. 
 On the day that Melanie is scheduled for dissection, a massive breach occurs at the military strong-hold and chaos ensues. Melanie manages to escape, along with Miss Justineau, Sergeant Parks, Dr. Caldwell and one of Parks's underlings. Together, they must find a way to survive outside the protective walls of their former bunker, avoiding roving bands of violent scavengers and unrestrained hungries, as they make their way to Beacon, one of the few human enclaves left in England. 
 Told in alternating points of view, The Girl With All The Gifts offers up a fresh take on the zombie genre. Melanie is a zombie, but she's fully sentient (though she has no memory of human life). She doesn't know what she is or why her circumstances vary so widely from the humans with whom she's now traveling. Dr. Caldwell is a borderline sociopath whose primary goal is to find a way to cut Melanie open as soon as she gets a chance. Helen Justineau is Melanie's primary defender, but even she can't deny what Melanie really is, even if Melanie seems capable of keeping her urges mostly in check. Sergeant Parks is just trying to keep everyone alive, which is proving to be more difficult than even he imagined. 
 I have never really considered myself a huge fan of the zombie genre, but I couldn't resist the idea of genius zombie kid. Luckily, I wasn't disappointed. This book hit all the right notes - the science of the zombie outbreak sounds plausible and the characters are all fully realized and morally complex. The pacing is nearly perfect and the denouement is both surprising and heart-wrenching. Fans of the zombie genre won't be disappointed; there's more than enough traditional zombie horror and gore to keep even the Romero-style zombie devotees happy. This is a fantastic books for adults and older teens who like a little philosophy with their blood and guts.

 I'm a little between 3 and 4 stars, but I didn't like this one as much as the first so I'm going with 3. The plot twist(s) were there, but I enjoyed/took by complete surprise the plot twists of the first book much, much more. The rest of my review here comprises a list of points I'd like to address in no particular order. It's a mixture of positive and negative, so really, 3 stars is the best fit. 
 1. Bromance. Locke and Jean are a great duo with lots of witty banter. They are also incredibly devoted to one another and in a life of thievery it's great to have one other incredibly skilled person at your back at all times. It's a partnership where I equally appreciate both characters. This novel expands their partnership a little further by introducing a female romantic interest. Said female is a great match for one of them, but how will the dynamic duo fare with a 3rd in their party? 
 2. Scheme after scheme. Locke and Jean start this one by planning to rob the world's most famous gambling house, the Sinspire. The Sinspire is crafted by Mr. Lynch to be a really interesting and impressive place to rob, so it's exciting to read about this. But Locke and Jean's scheming goes slightly off course by something, and of course our Gentlemen's Bastard's have to twist this aspect to go in their favor, so it ends up being a scheme on top of a scheme. As we keep going through the novel, more stuff comes up, and really I have to appreciate Mr. Lynch's planning to have all of this go through. It got a little confusing at times, however, just because there was so much going on, and Mr. Lynch's overly descriptive writing style isn't helping matters. In the end, I got the gist of it all, but things may have been more tense if I could've remembered/understood more of the details of the schemes. 
 3. Veering off course I wanted this header to have some sort of ship/pirate slang pun, but alas I am just not well enough versed in the field. In any case, the book felt a little too long. There was definitely some parts that felt like they weren't getting anywhere, and honestly I can't point out why they were all needed in the end (take me back to point 2, captain!). I think a lot of it was to include more pirate-y action, but I wasn't enjoying it, sadly. I really like the pirate characters Mr. Lynch created/introduced. They're unique and interesting in their own separate ways, but the pirates' conflicts just weren't all that exciting to me. With Locke and Jean's story being the main focus of the book, it felt like we didn't need as much seafaring action as was provided. It slightly felt like Mr. Lynch had a sudden need to write some Pirates of the Caribbean fanfiction and this is what we got. 
 Overall, there are some highlights to the book, but it ends up being a little too long and just slightly too much.

Carian Cole has been on my to read list for many months. I have a bit of a rockstar romance addiction and have heard nothing but good things about her books in the genre. The only reason for the delay has simply been too many books, too little time. I started seeing teasers for Talon several months before it came out, and was drawn to it for a number of reasons that I will bore my blog followers with and try to keep my review a little shorter here. Once I had a chance to read the synopsis, I was completely sold. I was so intrigued by the concept of the "social experiment" outlined....marry a stranger, agree to stay married for at least 6 months, journal about it and have video chats with the psychologist in charge. What could possibly go wrong?

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is definitely sf with its interest in the political and economic consequences of long-term cryosuspension (a bit also about its practical and medical aspects), falling into the subset of corporate malfeasance and investigation and proof of same (a whiff of businesspunk). Which I hadn't at all suspected from having heard the first chapter. Miles, now a father (and a good one by the sound of it) is off-planet investigating a shady business that may impact on Komarr. POVs include Miles, his long-suffering bodyguard Roic, and a local boy named Jin who doesn't know what he's stirred up, and only wants to take care of his animals. Enough POVs to skip boring stuff, and get interesting outside looks at Miles' luminescent personality; not so many to cause dizziness. The plot turned in ways I did not suspect, yet made for getting all the right people in the right places in a tightly written tango. 
 Spoiler: 
 But the heartbreak at the end, that was so neatly foreshadowed, undid me. Bujold, you bastard! You made me cry three times in five pages. I'm so used to your gradual epilogues, tying up neat ends that I'd forgotten about, not throwing in cliffs that have dropped out from under my feet.
You guys, I think that Philippa Gregory really believes that Elizabeth Woodville was a witch.

 Part Two of Remember When is very different from Part One as it doesn't have that carefree young adult feeling to it anymore and Trip and Layla are now dealing with the kind of issues grown-ups have... 
 Layla always chose to go the "sensible" route: she did it back in the day when she left Norman, NJ (and Trip Wilmington) for NYU, and ever since, she has tried to stay on that "sensible" and reasonable side of things doing what she thought was expected from her: taking a reasonable job, working hard for her promotion, getting engaged with her ambitious boyfriend and boss... Only she didn't expect that one event was going to throw her off in no time. 
 Trip Wilmington, now known to the public as Trip Wiley is back in town and Layla can't wait to meet him again, which she does under the pretense of interviewing him. And it turns out that although she remained in contact with him over the first few years of their separation until a total radio-silence from Trip's end, Trip and Layla still have that indescribable attraction to each other.

 There's a LOT going on in this debut novel, and some of it is pulled off better than other stuff. 
 Pluses: 
 --kick-ass protagonist. Tara is a young woman of color who's been expelled from a school of Craft (magic using power from the stars, souls, and other sources), who is hired by.... 
 --a kick-ass secondary character. Ms. Elayne Kevorian is a private investigator from a well-respected firm, who's been engaged to discover how and why a god named Kos has been killed. As it turns out, sometime in the past she had had a relationship with a ... 
 --kick-ass creepy character, which Did Not End Well. I pictured this guy as an evil George Clooney--smooth, manipulative, charming, but COLD underneath. He's representing clients who are protesting the provisions of Kos' "will," so to speak (commitments that the god made that must be honored upon his death). 
 --All of this action takes place in a port city called Alt Coulumb, which I pictured as a gothic Gotham--there are gargoyles on the buildings, and a central temple dedicated to Kos the Everburning, the recently departed god. I especially liked the details of the economics of this city, which many fantasy books overlook. The universe as a whole is a mishmash of vampires, god(esse)s, supernatural shapeshifters, humans, shades, etc., but I thought it worked. 
 Minuses: 
 --the uneven pacing. It never felt like the book settled down into a rhythm of steadily building tension, which is what you want in a mystery investigation. The switching POVs weren't always done well, either. 
 --the main character (Tara) was a bit of a Mary Sue. It didn't feel like she was in actual mortal danger sometimes. 
 --In the end, it didn't seem to me to be Tara's story at all. Turned out that two of the other characters were actually calling the shots behind the scenes. That's fine, and I've seen that done well, but it felt like a bit of a cheat, like Tara wasn't the hero of her own story. 
 I liked the universe, so I'm glad to see that this is the first in a series set there. I think the author shows great promise--I'll be interested to see what his later books are like (3 of them, at last count). I'd recommend this book to fans of fantasy, urban fantasy, and possibly paranormal romance, although that's not a particular focus of this book.

 The moment I started reading this script, I knew I was falling in love again. The heart and friendship of the Harry Potter series was shining through in the relationship of Albus and Scorpius and the magical world of the original series was alive once more. Harry Potter's son being sorted into Slytherin and becoming best friends with a Malfoy?  Sign me right up. The dynamic between the two leads was just silly, authentic, and ragtag enough to make them the perfect heroes. I would happily read a standalone series about their misadventures. The scene in which  the trio search for the time turner in Hermione's library  could have been taken straight out of the Harry Potter series. There was an absolute experience of joy that came with reading part one of this book. 
 It was during part two that things began to unravel. The joy that I was experiencing started to feel like I was forcing it along. The sense of wonder and cuteness started to wane, and the returning characters began to feel a bit different... a bit off. I began to question how much of J.K. Rowling was actually in this story. It seemed like the more plot-driven the story became, the more the characters seriously suffered and seemed more like roughly sketched characterizations of themselves rather than the actual Draco Malfoy or Hermione Granger. It was not only the characters who seemed to be from fan-fiction world, but there were so many instances of deus ex machina that I never feared anything for the characters. For example, after Draco conveniently had a limitless time-turner hidden the entire time  I realized that every obstacle from there on out would have an easy solution. I was right. This wasn't necessarily a bad thing, it kept the story stress-free and as a lighthearted and fun nostalgia trip. 
 Overall, this story served its purpose tremendously. I craved more from the Harry Potter universe and for a short while, I was granted another peek into a possible contemporary Hogwarts experience. I got another moment with characters I love, and was introduced to a couple more that I loved just as much. But if I were judging it as an actual installment in the Harry Potter canon, it would absolutely be the weakest in the series. As it is not, not really, I will judge it as a preview for the actual stageplay. It's got me intrigued and I would absolutely love to see it performed!

 So when we left off in the last book stuff had gotten real. Our group was taking hit after hit and it ended with Alex being broken by Ares but being spirited away and healed by Apollo. Like I said series. We finally know which god is behind things pulling all the strings and bent on war. Makes sense really. But as the mortal world starts to slip into chaos Alex has to reconcile what happened and shake herself doubt away and dive back into the fray. She will do anything necessary even work with a known enemy of the past to face the enemy of the present. All while trying to figure out a way out of this mess that lets her have her happily ever after in the end. 
 The options don't look good. Alex has been this strong force of nature through the books so far. She has had her moments of weakness and doubt sure but never like this. She actually wanted to die. Ares broke her. This is a hard hit to suffer. Aiden as always is there by her side willing to do anything to help. I love how supportive he is with her. Their connection from the start has always been off the charts but in this one it just really hits you in the core. There are so many moments where they just know the other and what they need on instinct or a single look. They are equals and always have been despite the breed order or her Apollyon powers they have always treated each other as equals. Both knowing the other is in danger and not trying to shut them away but instead trusting them and their ability to make it through. This really touches the heart. 
 Then we have Seth. I hated him. I didn't like him from the start but then I grew to hate his character and the evil he was a part of in his power hungry daze. I equated him with a rapist drugging her with the bond and then leeching her power even when she tried to say no. At the end of the last book with the showdown with Ares, all the pain, misery, and despair she felt as he broke her body and spirit I hoped he would feel every ounce through the bond. Let him take on the horror he brought on. He did. He is suddenly seeing through the haze of his power madness and wants to help, suddenly seeing the error of his ways. There was nothing he could do to redeem himself in my eyes. Though watching as he tried and meet skepticism and resistance from everyone else I enjoyed that. He got back on charm for so long seeing it not work, that everyone held him accountable for his evil deeds was refreshing. I liked that they never tried to belittle those deeds. 
 Now adding this into the story was huge story points but we still have a war to finish. This is the final book and there was a lot of ground to cover. We have to save the world and nothing is ever easy or without cost. This doesn't change here. There is a price to be demanded and no matter how hard or gut wrenching for the good of all our heroes will face it. I was constantly on the edge of my seat finishing this book trying to think of any twists or loop holes to make everything I wanted to happen to happen. There was a lot to cover and it wasn't smooth sailing and in war people die. This book actually had me getting teary and/or crying in different parts just thinking about certain characters futures (yes I know vague me) and this got more intense the closer we got to the end. 
 I was so nervous as I got closer that it might not end in a way that satisfied me. I should not have worried though because JLA knows what she's doing and this series was amazing. It hits you with all the feels and then some but you end feeling complete. Like how it ends you can instantly see it from the start looking back on the whole journey. It also did something that I wasn't sure was possible given how I felt about Seth pre this book and that's make me want to read his spin-off/sequel series. I think I'm going to hold off a few months before I start these but I have the first three ready to go. While there is the spin-off/sequel series I think the Covenant series wraps up nicely in Sentinel and I highly recommend it.

So, it needs to be said: I generally like adaptations. I'm the type of person who will willingly read or watch any adaptation of classic stories, no matter how bad - I'm looking at you, From Prada to Nada - simply because I like seeing new interpretations of classic stories that I already love. 
 With that being said, I generally don't expect all that much from these adaptations. The story's already been told, it's just in a different genre/outfit/whatever. So when I heard about Great, and how it was an adaptation of The Great Gatsby, I figured I'd like it, but wouldn't be blown away by it. 
 I was wrong. Great is a fantastic, timely adaptation that is not only a great spin on a classic tale, but also the sign of a fantastic new voice to the YA world. (Yes, I'm talking about you, Sara!) 
 Naomi Rye is the daughter of a divorced high school coach father, and a famous Food Network star mother. As a part of their divorce settlement, Naomi is forced to spend time with her mom in the Hamptons each summer, which typically means hanging out with rich, monied people that she has nothing in common with. 
 However, Naomi just happens to make the acquaintance of elusive fashion blogger Jacinta, who quickly takes Naomi into her fold. While Naomi is initially intimated (and awed) by the amount of money that Jacinta lavishes on her parties and the people around her, she quickly realizes that Jacinta actually has a past and secrets to hide. 
 It's not that easy creating an original character when you're reinterpreting a classic tale, but Naomi is absolutely original in her own right. Benincasa has made her smart and thoughtful, but also snarky and self-depricating about a world that she clearly isn't going out of her way to fit into. 
 However, she's also adaptable. When Naomi does make the acquaintance of the elusive, highly-sought after Jacinta, she doesn't go out of her way to befriend her or impress her. Instead, Naomi shows Jacinta genuine friendship and compassion. In turn, Jacinta shows her a vulnerability that not only wins over Naomi, but will likely win over readers as well. 
 Benincasa remains fairly loyal to Fizgerald's original story throughout Great - down to the inclusion of a very famous scene where Jacinta shows Delilah just what she's been able to afford now, and Delilah reacts accordingly - but doesn't also fail to put her own spin on the classic tale. She also includes probing and thoughtful questions on wealth, societal pressures like drinking and bullying, and the difficulties of growing up in such a monied, high-stakes world, all of which I think readers will absolutely be fascinated by, and relate to. 
 All in all, Great pulled me into the story from the very first page, and kept me riveted until the final denouement. Even though I already knew how the story was going to end - I figured that Beninancasa wouldn't stray from the source enough to change it - I was still surprised to realize just how moved I was by that ending. That, in my mind, is a clear sign that Benincasa has written an adaptation that should be regarded in its own right. 
 Of special note: I highly, highly appreciated the fact that Benincasa does incorporate several LGBT romances into Great, without any specific emphasis on the fact that they're LGBT. It's not only extremely true and reflective of the real world, but also just made my reading experience richer in general. I can only hope that more YA writers will follow in her footsteps. 
 *** 
 Final verdict: 
 Great was in a word, great. Benincasa has written an adaptation of The Great Gatsby that is true and loyal to the original, while adding the sort of details and personal touches that also makes the story highly relevant and timely for the 21st century. 
 I highly recommend Great for fans of contemporary YA fiction, but also for fans who are looking for something new in their reading habits. As for me, I'll absolutely be back for anything else that Benincasa may write.

Reader thoughts: Very funny! VVV knows how to wield a pen and tell quirky stories with the resonance of old fairytales. Little Red Riding Hood retold from the pov of the cloak? So fun! Or retold with a mixmash of stories gone wrong, ruined by the interference of a kind, short-sighted woodcutter? Ha! 
 Actually, I had to read the short-sighted woodcutter one to my roommate, and she thought it was horrifically morbid. The man didn't know he was accidentally helping the wolf by mistake. He didn't know he was accidentally helping a witch catch Hansel and Gretel. He was just a kind old man. 
 Writer thoughts: It's quite ingenious, really, to take the same story and tell it over and over again and somehow make it fresh and interesting every time. It really shows VVV's diverse writing skills. 
 It also shows how well she can think abstractly, and like a philosopher. You could say that each author to write a retelling must capture the essence of the original (like chair-ness) in order to recreate it in a new way.

I often end up with mixed feelings about novels based on fairy tales, and this retelling of one my old favorites, The Twelve Dancing Princesses, is no exception. 
 I liked Azalea's interactions with her sisters, and I especially liked that she seemed to mature as the story went on. Unfortunately the story was so packed with princesses and suitors that only the heroine got much attention. One of the secondary relationships was adorable, but the main romance felt tacked on. 
 The princesses got caught up in a cycle of sneaking away, being tired, and getting into trouble with little other movement in the plot. It all started to feel like "dance, rinse, repeat." The antagonist took a turn for the menacing in the end, but that mostly made me wish he'd managed more than blandly creepy earlier. 
 The setting was interesting and well-described, and the author did a good job of revealing details slowly. Certain other aspects of the writing didn't work for me, though. Moments of pretty fairy-tale prose kept clashing up against modern slang, and things tended to get muddy during the action scenes. 
 I guess I like it best when adaptations go deep into the characters or add an unexpected twist to a classic story, and despite its promise, this one really didn't do either of those things.

Gaelen Foley is an author who inspires so much ambivalence in me. While reading one of her books I will move from disgust to disbelief to resignation to pleasure to frustration and more. Some parts of her books are really good. Then the heroine does a doormat or TSTL move and I think: it's all over, red rover. I read on and lo! The hero stops being a dick long enough for me to start to like him, and I am engaged again. 
 That pretty much summed up my feelings about this one, #5 from the Knight Miscellany -strange name- series. 
 I initially really didn't like the hero, Devlin. He was so consumed with his plan to avenge the deaths of his family that he had lost all self-respect and basically saw the whole thing as a suicide mission. Of course, he reluctantly falls in love with Lizzie, the fairly bland character we met in previously in the series, and starts to discover a new lust for life- and, well, a whole lot of just lust, too. 
 The story was a good one and GF manages to create quite a complex plot with great characterisations, especially of the villains, who are defs a ghastly bunch of nobs. Their lifestyle would probably have killed them eventually anyway, but Devlin desperately wanted to hasten their demise. 
 I found it hard to accept the fact that Devlin couldn't let go of his need for revenge, until I realised that he saw himself as somehow responsible for the deaths of his parents and sister and was on a massive guilt trip. 
 Lizzie seemed a bit too good to be true, initially, and she annoyed me, but then she loved Dev and was always prepared to give him a chance to explain himself and try to be a better person. That is actually a very admirable quality. So many HR's feed off mistrustful MCs to generate the big Misunderstanding that drives the angst in the relationship. Sometimes, it is actually pleasant to find MCs who really try to believe the best in each other and work together to overcome their obstacles rather than creating even bigger ones, by always jumping to the worst possible conclusions. Sure, if to turns out he WAS unfaithful- kick him to the kerb. Hard. But let's wait and see if there is another explanation. 
 There was a very dramatic and violent climax to the story (lots of blood and stuff) but I loved how the two women held their own in the end, proving to be just as resourceful, courageous and strong as the men. 
 I have now read Lord of Ice and Lady of Desire in this series, too. It took a while but I did end up liking Damien from Lord of Ice. Jacinda' vapid silliness just drove me nuts in Lady of Desire. 
 People rave about The Duke, but a few have slammed the hero's disgusting, sexist treatment of the heroine, (who is apparently a courtesan, which is never a trope I like), so I may not get to that one. I think Lucien in Lord of Fire sounds like a bit of a pig, too, but maybe GF can turn these guys around into men I actually like. (She may well struggle to do that for Alec in One Night of Sin!) 
 She has, however, succeeded in doing that for me so far. Devil takes a Bride was bloody good read- well worth the 4 stars!

Okay, I'll admit it: The blurb on this novel didn't win me over. 
 But since author Jessica Park raved about Aspen on her Facebook page, I decided to give it a chance--especially when I saw that it was available through NetGalley. And the rest, as they say, is history. 
 This powerful narrative of self-discovery, friendship, and love completely blew me away. Aspen, our heroine, is a phenomenal character. But the secondary characters are equally compelling. While I can certainly accept this as a standalone, I'd love to see a sequel featuring Kim and Cass (with glimpses of Ben, Ninny, and Aspen, of course). 
 The first thing I noticed about Crane's novel was its realistic portrayal of teenagers and the high school experience. The author establishes a disparity between Aspen's perception of herself and how others see her, which--while always the case to some degree--is perhaps most evident during these formative years. 
 Aspen is notably insecure regarding her appearance, especially her hair--"the curly, dirty blonde mess that protrudes from my head, like a perm on a troll doll"--which prevents her from blending in with her peers. Nevertheless, she is relatively content with her status on campus: While she has a small group of loyal friends, she's not what anyone would term popular--that is, until an unfortunate accident catapults her into unwelcome stardom. 
 Navigating this new phenomenon only adds to her list of problems, which already consists of dealing with stress-induced migraines, processing her reaction to the trauma, and hallucinating a dead person. So her emphasis on using the right word(s) is indicative of a need to restore order to a chaotic, unpredictable life. After all, definitions are black and white (quite literally, in fact, if one considers how they're printed on a dictionary page). 
 Readers are kept in suspense regarding the real story behind the accident, and it's only through the combined effort of Aspen, her newfound friends, and her therapist, that our title character is able to piece together the night's events. 
 One of my favorite aspects of the novel is the witty dialogue that takes place between Aspen and her friends, and between Aspen and Ben. I laughed out loud at how unexpected and comical some of these conversations were. (If only I could be so clever! Alas, I'm unsure how to cultivate or hone this skill.) But beyond being funny, these exchanges demonstrate how smart, well-informed, and good-natured this cast of characters is at its core. 
 For me, Aspen is the perfect balance of light and heavy. Both Ninny's eccentricity and the playful banter between characters seem to counter the novel's darker moments, while the supportive Suzy and Kim counteract the venomous Olivia and Claire. In addition, Aspen treats concepts such as identity, friendship, romance, and family with the honesty and reverence they deserve. 
 Overall, Aspen is a gripping, emotional read that is so real, so profound in its simplicity, that it will have you reading compulsively until the very last page.

 I know quite a few people didn't enjoy book one in this series, Uninvited, but I absolutely loved it. Most people weren't happy that there wasn't an explanation provided about the HTS gene and how that is even supposed to work. But I'm the girl who enjoys superhero movies, if I was going to sit there and question the actual science behind them then I wouldn't enjoy them half as much. Sometimes you just have to enjoy the story for what it is, a piece of fiction. My review for Uninvited was really glowing, I was completely won over by all of the action, but also by the romance between Davy and Sean. So imagine my surprise when the plot summary for book two doesn't even mention Sean once. I was not happy with that and I became very nervous to start this book, especially with the mention of a new male character, I began to worry that this was going to turn into another horrid love triangle book and I was not looking forward to it. 
 I wish that I was able to say that I enjoyed Unleashed just as much as I did Uninvited, but I would most definitely be lying. I was so disappointed by this book and part of me really wishes that I hadn't read it and had just made up my own conclusion to this duology. We come into the story right where book one left off, Davy and the others have managed to escape the training camp and are about to make the crossing into Mexico. It's painfully obvious from the blurb that she's not going to be sticking with these guys for too long, and that happens by about page 70. Davy finds herself in trouble and is rescued by a guy who just happens to be part of a resistance cell and is going to go out of his way to save her from everything. 
 When I realise a books going to be ALL romance. 
 What I really liked about book one was the fact that the romance in it wasn't the main focus. I've said time and time again that I don't mind romance in my reads, as long as that romance only takes up a small part of the plot. Uninvited did this well, the romance was there but it was more of a slow build and wasn't the focus of the story. I liked that I couldn't put the book down because it had a lot of action to it. As Unleashed was the concluding book to the series, I assumed it would be packed full of action and I'd be reading into the early hours of the morning, unable to put the book down. I couldn't have been more wrong, this book became all about the romance. What makes that a million times more frustrating is the fact it's a completely new romance to book one. Maybe some authors can pull of introducing an entirely new love interest and get you to suddenly root for them, but this did not work here. 
 I liked Davy in book one, by the end she was becoming strong and didn't constantly need Sean to keep jumping in and rescuing her. I didn't like that we suddenly have a new guy show up who feels the need to constantly jump in and save her. You'd also think that being part of the group that's trying to take down the Wainwright Agency that Davy would get to play some role in this. She doesn't. Everything happens without her because she's too busy having yet another romance storyline with a guy I don't really care for. I was hoping for action, suspense and twists and turns, what I got was romance and melodrama.

Book one was really good, it was one of my favourite reads last year, and there's nothing more disappointing then when the conclusion to a series doesn't live up to your expectations. I received this book filled with excitement, so sure that I was going to absolutely love it. But, quite honestly, my feelings can be summed up in one gif: 
 Yay, this is going to be epic. Lets get my celebratory cake ready! Wait.... what? What? Ehhhhh, f*ck this sh*t.

While J.D. Hawkins isn't new to me as a person, this is the first book of his I've read. I did try to read some of his other stuff, but for whatever reason, I wasn't able to connect with those books. I'd heard good things about this one, that it was different from his previous work, so I thought I'd give it a go. 
 I'm glad I did. 
 This is a friends-to-lovers story and while there were some aspects that left me scratching my head, over all, I liked it. 
 Margo was a great character. Though some parts of her were confounding. For a person who was so wild in college, being only three years out, she certainly changed a lot. Gone were the parties and ONS and immature behavior-well, mostly on that one. She was looking to have a career and settle down in her personal life. Which is fine. That is totally cool. However, from how she was described in college to how she's read in the present, CollegeMargo felt like a completely different character from CareerMargo. I know people can change, but her change was fast and absolute. Still, in spite of that, I liked her. I liked that she was super smart and not the stereotypical female lead. I didn't hate being in her head, and for a male writer penning her, I enjoyed the things she thought about. The way her mind worked and she analysed things. It was nice to experience. 
 Owen was great too. For being a manwhore, I'm glad we don't see that. Yes we see him on dates, but from the way those played out, I think he was trying to live up to a reputation he stopped having when college ended. Because he really would have tapped into the fountain at work otherwise. I loved his friendship with Margo and how in so many ways, while we see her contemplating relationship status with Owen, it's actually Owen who falls all in first. Even if it did take a big shake up to make him realise it. He was clever and enjoyable. Though I was a bit put-off by the sex scenes. He just didn't seem the type to be that commanding. It's not bad, I just did't expect him to be that way in the bedroom. I actually imagined him sweet with a naughty side. Oh well. 
 Louise was a great side character. I'd love to know more about her. Manny was a hoot! Definitely need more from him. Especially for as whorish as he is, he knows not to ruin a good thing. I do wish there was more resolution with Owen's father. And since I did read the extra epilogue, I wonder when the relationship was repaired enough to warrant his (and Nancy's) 
 presence on the rock. Or even how Louise got her role.  
 I liked the ending. It did feel a bit abrupt, making everything nice and tidy quickly. And I did read the extra epilogue because I felt like there was more to the story, more need for closure. Though it's six months into the future, I do wish we could have had a little more time. 
 Though the proposal was a nice touch. But again, I still felt like there was more that needed to be said.

I think this is the first Hercule Poirot I've read, and I'm both pleased and disappointed this was my first Poirot. 
 As usual, Christie does a marvelous job of laying out the plot and the details and sewing them all together into a unified, coherent conclusion. And I think to a less picky reader, Murder on the Orient Express would be a five-star read. But there were a couple of things about this one that I didn't like, despite my overall enjoyment of the novel. 
 First, I actually figured out who committed the murder before the end of the book. Which surprised me, I haven't actually been able to do that very often with Dame Agatha. Generally I'm not able to deduce the ending before hand, so that was a little disappointing because that's one of the things I enjoy about Agatha Christie novels--her ability to stump me. 
 Second, the ending. Without giving too much away, I thought the decision of Poirot, Bouc, and Dr. Constantine at the very end of the novel compromised the presentation of justice Christie had set up through Poirot earlier in the novel. It annoyed me, but I also saw the logic of it, as well. Allowing the legal system to decide the matter would have been a long, complicated process due to the nature of the crime, however my own sense of morality insists that Poirot made the wrong choice. 
 That said, I really did like the book, and I can see why this is considered one of Agatha Christie's finest novels. It hasn't usurped Sleeping Murder as my favorite Christie novel, but then again I highly doubt anything ever will.

At the beginning, it's mostly a cluster of behind-the-scenes anecdotes about what really goes on in hotels; by the end, the book is basically an account the author's existential crisis as he realizes he's stuck in a love-hate relationship with the hotel industry. 
 I particularly enjoyed the chapters about his time in the "Bellvue" in New York City, which is a fascinating case study of employer/employee relationships. When he's writing about things he's passionate about, he's really engaging. 
 At times the writing made me cringe, not because it's bad but because every once in a while Tomsky writes like an obnoxious frat boy. At one point, for example, he's quoting an Asian guest and he renders their sentences by substituting "r" for "l" throughout. Seriously? And sometimes he's sexist in a clueless, har-har way. Yuck. However, he also states his obvious disapproval of racist, misogynist, or homophobic guest or employee/er behaviour, so I have to conclude that he's just sort of clueless, not malicious. 
 So I guess overall this is a sort of uneven, but extremely entertaining first book. If he writes another one, I will read it! 
 PS I was SOOOO curious about the identities of the celebrities and the NYC hotel that he writes about pseudonymously. Here's what I found through Edward Sung's blog entry on the book: 
 The jerky 1980s teen movie star is probably John Cusack. 
 The really nice Mr. H. is probably Dustin Hoffman. 
 The real "Bellvue Hotel" is probably the Parker Meridien Hotel in New York.

I have a hangover...a Bourbon hangover! Oooooweeeee! That books was just SO much. I am telling you---if you want to be entertained, gripped, and turning pages like a maniac THIS is the book for you. 
 This was like Dallas and Dynasty and Falcon Crest all rolled into one and set in the heart of Kentucky's high society. The world that is created in this story is one that is almost unimaginable. The cast of characters are people you will recognize from movies, tv shows and books that you've watched and read in the past. They are all cliches we know and love (or hate). 
 This is a story about a family whose reputation is all an illusion. While the rest of the country sees a family of rich, successful, good looking people...really their core is rotten and this first installment of the new series, that rot starts to seep through to the surface. 
 Tulane Baldwine (Lane) and Lizzie King fell in love two years before the story starts. But Lane's poor decision making led to them splitting and both of them have spent that time, pining and not moving on from each other. 
 When Lane is called home to see to the one of the only people in the world he loves, he and Lizzie are forced to confront each other and their feelings for each other. They have a lot to deal with. The woman who Lane considers his mother  I hated that there had to be Mammy in this story  is ill, his estranged wife is scheming and his father is just utterly evil! 
 Lane's arrival at home coincides with Derby weekend. This is Charlemont society's biggest weekend of the year and the Baldwine's lunch on the day of the Derby is one of the most anticipated events of the weekend. No expense is spared and the entire staff at Easterly, the Baldwine's massive estate, is working at full throttle to make sure things go off without a hitch. 
 But, as the day of the event nears, the facade the family shows the world starts to crack and as those cracks widen it becomes clear that the trickle of odd occurrences is prelude to a deluge of holy hell that will turn the family and everyone who is affiliated with it upside down and inside out. 
 The family's patriarch William Baldwine is the king of villains. He is a selfish, cruel and feckless man. Nothing is sacred to him. He sees his children as disposable pawns and his wife as necessary encumbrance. The tangled web he has woven starts to prove itself incapable of supporting his weight. His grotesque and unbelievably cruel actions start to come to light and boy, they are a doozy 
 We meet 2 of Lane's three siblings, Edward and Virgina ("Gin"). From the flashbacks to their childhood, I found it miraculous that Lane managed to be a relatively stable and functional adult. 
 His siblings, not so much. Lane's brother Edward, who I think is my favorite character, has been brought low by what is initially referred to as "his tragedy" and he is trying to rebuild his life-- away from his family. He will have to decide whether he will live in an alcohol induced haze for the rest of his life or if he step in to help his family when they need him. It also appears that he might actually have a little love triangle happening in his book... 
 "Gin" has never really grown up. She lives in a fantasy world where she has never really had to deal with any consequences for her behavior. Well in the space of a few short days her reckoning comes demanding full and immediate payment and she is pockets to let. She is incredibly self destructive and I'll be watching to see if her love interest (Sam. T--delish) will be able to help her save herself in the next book, but in this story things don't look that good for Gin. 
 The intrigue is off the charts and as the family hurtles from crisis to crisis, we realize that what we know so far is just the tip of the iceberg. Although Lane and Lizzie's story is resolved at the end of the book, the family's story is not and the hints of what's to come left me feeling like I had drunk a whole bottle of bourbon all by myself. I can't wait for the next installment!

How do you define love? Can it be done? Perhaps it can't be summed up in one word as so many people are led to think but something that belongs to all words and to the silence that falls between them. 'The Lover's Dictionary' is a story of "You" and "I" and seeking words that touch on so many sensations which aren't easily captured. 
 I'd wanted to get my hands on a copy of this for a while. The other day, I made a random decision to see what books by David Levithan my local bookstore had in stock and because of Valentine's Day, 'The Lover's Dictionary' was available. I snatched it up. 
 'The Lover's Dictionary' is a novel but not one that flows in the usual way, through chapters or sequential events. Instead, it is written in first person by the unnamed "I" under a variety of words, be they nouns, verbs and/or adjectives and adverbs. Instead of writing of love as a general subject, he tells the story of his relationship with "You", whose name and gender are never specified. 
 Despite only getting snatches of the relationship, without too many overbearing details, I felt that I was gaining a very personal insight. 'The Lover's Dictionary' treads the line between diary and love letter. It shows the narrator's feelings and reflections but he is writing to his lover throughout. It is a story which they share and have written together. 
 What is wonderful about the format of the novel is that it shows the relationship people have with words as much as they do with each other. When you first learn to speak and comprehend what a word means, you have no clue of its definitions. You just pick things up through context. Even now, I would be hard-pressed to recite an exact definition of a specific word. 'The Lover's Dictionary' defines words in a way which applies to how we feel and what we do and how words relate to the things we go through. 
 The book is a short read length-wise but one you linger on, whether when you're reading it or afterwards. The story isn't a tale of everyone's love. It is a specific couple and their struggles and sentiments. What 'The Lover's Dictionary' achieves is an insight into the difficulties and delights of making that connection with a specific person. "You" and "I" could be anyone and the story leaves room for the reader to wonder and reflect. 
 I would be quick to recommend this book to those looking for a romance novel but not one that gushes and grieves. I always appreciate writing that makes an impact without trying to punch you in the gut. 
 Perhaps next, I'll read The Devil's Dictionary...or more books by David Levithan.

Oh boy, Real has got to be one of the best books of the year. 
 Yes, I'm late to the Remy party, but I'm here and and I could not be more excited! This book was intense, fun and heart-wrenching. Remington "Riptide" Tate is not like everyone else, he cannot control his anger or mood swings, and most of those who see his darker side fear him. Enter Brooke. She cannot help but be drawn to this enigmatic guy. For their own reasons neither Brooke nor Remy will give into their passion at first. Don't fret though, it was not one of those frustrating cat and mouse chases. Yes, they have their ups and downs, which their passion fuels, but it is all worth the wait. Their journey was so enthralling, I couldn't predict what anyone was going to do, but I could not wait to find out! 
 "Because I hate what he does to me. I hate that I want him like this, I hate that I feel so volatile, I want to tear his eyes out and then go cry about it." 
 ~Brooke 
 Remy has finally found someone he can trust, that won't hurt him, and that truly understands and loves him without question. Brooke has had a rough go after graduating college, but Remy fixes her unemployment problem. Before Brooke even starts to work with Remy he has become so much more than her employer. Remy and Brooke have this instant connection, and hold great protectiveness for each other. Finally, we see a story where the woman is just as, if not more, fiercely protective of her man. She even goes to the lengths of protecting him from those he has known for years. They share their secrets with one another, and refuse to let anyone in their bubble. Brooke provides a security for Remy and saves him from himself and others unlike anyone else in his life... but she also evokes those darkest feelings and urges that she has to save him from. Their relationship is a lot of give and take, and Brooke has to force him to see reason more than once. They don't just connect on an emotional level, their time between the sheets is HOT! There were quite a few time where I had put my ereader down and control my blushing. Brooke and Remy have found equals in each other and I am so excited to see where their journey leads them. 
 "I want you to be my fucking REAL." 
 ~Remy 
 The circumstances behind Real are very intriguing. It is rare that we see an author take on, what some might call a stigma such as the one discussed in Real, and it is done beautifully no less. It was not just a gloss over point, Katy Evans digs deep behind the why and how with Remy and still writes a very captivating story that I loved. She conveys such raw emotions it will make your heart ache... in a good way :) These characters made me feel their pain and happiness and by the end I was completely invested in their lives. I am so thrilled this will be an ongoing series and we will see more of Remy and Brooke!

I gave this book two stars because of the strengths it shares with the first two books in the series: it's intriguing, has fascinating characters, and has a unique plot and setting (rural western Virginia rather than a big city or beach town). But unlike the first two books in The Raven Cycle, Blue Lily, Lily Blue has flaws that are difficult to overlook this time, the most important being that this is clearly a book of fillers. 
 After a book as well-executed (in this reviewer's opinion) as The Dream Thieves, it was almost jarring to see how erratic the pacing was this time around. Rather than answering questions presented in the last book, BLLB instead introduces new questions that are clearly left open so that they can come up again in the last book. Of all the stories effected by this, Adam's suffers the most. We are reminded on virtually every page that he was abused, but we never actually learn anything about his life before Aglionby or anything that really defines him beyond his abuse--for a character that fixes cars like a pro, is intelligent and well-read, and is acutely aware of all that is going on around him, this is especially disappointing. His trial scene is perhaps the most frustrating: after vaguely worrying about facing his father in court, Adam is spontaneously joined by his friends--how they found out about the case and managed to somehow show up precisely as the trial began is not revealed--only to have the scene cut off and the verdict not revealed, neither by thought or conversation, in the hundred pages that follow.* This is only made worse by Adam's constantly shifting thoughts and emotions throughout the second half of the novel. For a fairly outwardly collected character, this creates an awkward advancement, and his "awakening" at the novel's conclusion feels rushed and out of place. 
 Although I'd argue that each of the main characters is still lovable in their own way, it's more difficult to sympathize with the group at this point. Despite being arguably the most heavily focused on character, Blue is also quickly becoming one of the series' weakest points. Despite telling us herself in the first book that she's clearly a judgmental person, Blue is never called out for her actions. She is extremely critical of both Gansey and Adam, often unreasonably, but is never urged to apologize or admit that she is wrong. Her romantic relationship with Gansey--which we are told from day one is destined to be true love--is still rather unconvincing. Surprisingly, Adam and Ronan's relationship, which isn't even yet canon, is more believable than our other pair's: we've seen them talk, argue, interact around other people as well as the paranormal, do mundane tasks such as going to class or to the grocery store, and confide in each other. By contrast, Gansey and Blue only spend time alone together when it's in the romantic context, and neither seem to really know anything about each other that the other characters don't know already. Their love story is an forced one, and it's hard to see how two characters so fundamentally different from one another (especially when one party--Blue--critiques the other to the point that arguably borders on mistreatment) could have a long-lasting relationship. 
 Lastly, BLLB does nothing to establish why we should care about the characters' mystical quest in the first place. Cabeswater still doesn't have much of a purpose, and why on Earth anyone would want to wake up Glendower is a mystery, since we're given no reason for why he needs to be woken or what he's going to do once he's awake. Then there is The Grey Man, a hit man who is apparently in the midst of a redemption arc despite never showing any remorse, and who is shown universal respect by the other characters despite having been the one who killed Ronan's father. 
 The truth of the matter is, if you enjoyed the first two books and adore the characters, as I do, you'll still enjoy reading BLLB. But once the original read is finished, there's no denying that it could have been better. 
 *Update: to further elaborate on why the trial scene particularly bothered me so much, there were several reasons: 
 1) It was probably the biggest deux ex machina in the series thus far. Gansey and Ronan show up precisely as Adam's trial begins, and there's really no clue as to how they found out that the trial was that day. It's clear that the author set this up for emotional impact, but the level of happenstance prevents it from being very effective. 
 2) As many other people have mentioned, Adam has some sort of epiphany in this scene where he decides that Gansey was right all along and that he only wants to help Adam out because they're friends, not as a means to control him. This certainly sounds great, but it also (probably unintentionally) puts all the blame on Adam. Gansey may be a nice guy, but he has he flaws too, and to portray all their disagreements as Adam's fault is frustrating and unfulfilling. 
 3) Out of everything that happened in this book, what bothered me the most was how Ms. Stiefvater decided to have Gansey be a friend of the judge presiding over the case. We see Gansey come swaggering in, shaking the judge's hand, making small talk about their home lives, and doing his politician charade. We know that Adam was assaulted, so again we're supposed to think this is a great thing, for Gansey to defend his abused friend. However, what we rather get is an example of a wealthy teenager using power and wealth to influence a legal case. The verdict sits on the fact that Gansey Has Connections, and not on Adam, who is doing something incredibly brave and heart-breaking. It also seems like the author is glorifying this use of power, and simply because we already know and care about Gansey doesn't make this any less disturbing.

ORIGINAL POST: RULES OF CIVILITY by Amor Towles: Best Friends for Now 
 http://fangswandsandfairydust.com/201... on August 12, 2015 
 ARC obtained anonymously at BEA. No remuneration was exchanged and all opinions presented herein are my own except as noted. 
 I picked this book up anonymously at BEA. Frankly it sat on my shelf and I didn;t think I would get to it during my blogging career. But, someone chose it for my book club so here I am. It is "literary fiction," so is probably intended to be critiqued in all sorts of esoteric manners. 
 This book is about a lot of things. Like a contemporary romance featuring youngish people, the times were tough, people were on the end of the Great Depression and an economic relapse and on the verge of WWII (with forays into the Spanish Civil War). Social roles were changing and our classless society was both stratifying and dissolving. Like the books wherein people in their 20s and 30s try to find direction in contemporary times, this book deals with similar choices and issues. It also nods to great writers of the story's time period (pre-WWII): Fitzgerald, Rand, Parker, etc. 
 Have you ever had friends you thought you would have forever, the friends you thought really knew you to the bottom of your soul and you them? I'm not talking about the girls you met at sleep-away camp when you were teens, but the friend you met as an adult, who you treated as a sister, and who then blew you off, or who inexplicably changed personalities? This story, for me spoke directly to the fickle nature of some friendship; especially as we become adults. 
 I felt as if this book rambled a lot: at times I thought it wasn't really going anywhere. But one thing leads to another, one "minor" encounter can have remarkably long lasting effects. It was unusual in its punctuation; avoiding those pesky quotation marks. 
 Katey is something interesting: well read, smart, amply skilled in shorthand and such, clever, with ambiguous morals. If she had been a man at the time, the world would have been her oyster. But, as one woman tells her in the book she shouldn't worry about what the guy she ends up with is going to do, but what she is going to do. 
 It was one of those times when the pendulum was swinging forward for women, and society women were more hampered by norms than the women who had built themselves up from nothing were. Katey had no expectations from friends or family -- she appears to have had neither between her father's death and the time of the story. In a sense she is a blank slate upon which the twentieth century gets to write its story of what a working woman is. She is also without a social past, and through coincidence becomes like a visitor to another planet as she enters social circles higher than those of her birth and status. 
 While unquestionably Katey is the heroine of this story, she is morally ambiguous. She isn't a bad person, but she's no Mother Theresa. 
 This is the second book in one week I read about the same period of time, with the other occurring in England. I felt in each though that the women were dispassionate, husks really, waiting for a man, or at least love, to make their lives begin. Of course each learns that is not how one's life is made complete but it is the premium toppings on the sundae. 
 Katey has the sense to go on living and progressing without the necessity of a man, although she still has the tendency towards wanting one. But, getting in on the ground floor of a new magazine, she is the "new woman;" like Katherine Hepburn in a slew of movies (although her popularity was a little later), she could become the first Helen Gurley Brown if she stayed focused. 
 The "Rules of Civility' refer to a text attributed to George Washington setting forth rules every young man should aspire to follow. 
 But this book is about a lot of things -- some are obvious and others are not. I found it slow to start but easy to read. And, I find I keep thinking about it and what it means. It is strange and modern, and yet ordinary and classic. Highly recommend.
