Colin Singleton is a child prodigy, convinced that as he ages, he becomes less remarkable with each passing day. While able to converse in eleven different languages and capable of memorising the majority of everything he reads (for hours every day), he's not really able to adapt the reading into anything new - like a true genius would be able to. He desperately wants to make some sort of significant contribution to the world, even more so after he's crushed when dumped by his girlfriend on the day of their high school graduation. 
 Not that he should be unused to being dumped. While Colin is fairly actively unpopular in school, he has nonetheless dated (however briefly) and been dumped by eighteen different girls called Katherine. Katherine 19, his most recent girlfriend, is in fact also Katherine 1, who asked him to be her boyfriend when they were children, and then promptly broke up with him not long after. Since they'd been going out for nearly a year by the time she dumped him again as a teenager (by far his longest relationship), I don't think Colin should complain. He's devastated, causing his only friend, Hassan, to decide they need to go on a summer road trip to make Colin happy again. The fact that Hassan is willing to take time out of his busy life slacking off, watching Judge Judy, is clearly a great sacrifice on his part. 
 The boys end up in the little town of Gutshot, Tennessee, where apparently the Arch Duke Franz Ferdinand of Austria is buried (his body having been bought and brought over in the 1930s). They meet Lindsey Lee Wells (as well has her boyfriend, the Other Colin and his friends) and are hired by her mother, who owns and runs the local factory (where they make tampon strings!) to compile an oral history of Gutshot. She'll pay them 500 dollars a week as well as room and board. Colin is determined that his great contribution to the world will be The Theorem of Underlying Katherine Predictability, which will successfully predict the future and outcome of any romantic relationship, a mathematical formula worked out based on his history with Katherines 1 through 19. He's also convinced that if he can just get the theorem to work, he'll be able to persuade Katherine 19 to take him back. Colin may have an IQ of over 200, but he's really not very good at figuring out human nature. 
 Having decided that I needed to read ALL the John Green YA novels after completing Will Grayson, Will Grayson, I decided to start with the one that had the lowest Goodreads rating. I kept waiting for this book to stop exasperating me and entertain me in the way the other John Green books I'd read did. In the end, there was more I liked than disliked, but I'm glad this is a book I borrowed from the library rather than own myself. 
 What I liked: 
 - Hassan (except for that unfortunate brief while when he decided he wanted to refer to himself as Daddy constantly). Colin's best (and only) friend. A chubby Muslim who occasionally attempts to convert Colin to Islam, Hassan appears to have no major life goals, except slack off and watch Judge Judy all day. He has made it his mission to notify Colin every time he gets carried away with spouting trivia, so that his friend can at least attempt to fit in with his teenage peers. He's also quite unamused with Colin's hang-up on Katherines and wants to help his buddy move on, perhaps meet and like a girl NOT named Katherine. 
 - Lindsey Lee Wells. Lindsey was fun, and her bad taste in boyfriends withstanding (spoiler - the Other Colin, the most popular guy in school isn't all that nice). She, like the majority of the inhabitants in Gutshot, seems to have no real desire to ever leave the town, despite her mother's dreams for her to go off to college. She's incredibly well-liked by pretty much everyone in town, but has many of the self-esteem issues that seem to plague so many teenage girls. 
 One of the criticisms I've read of John Green is that he always writes Manic Pixie Dream Girls in his books. Based on the books I've read so far, that seems deeply unfair. Neither Jane in Will Grayson, Will Grayson, nor Lindsey in this seemed very MPDG. I think the only character I can think that applies, to a certain extent, is Augustus Waters in The Fault in Our Stars, who can be said to have quite a bit of the Manic Pixie Dream Boy about him. But I digress, back to my list: 
 - The footnotes. Yup, this book has a number of footnotes. Sometimes they are there to give a translation of the Arabic, French or German occasionally spoken by the characters, but most of the time, they seem to just be there to interject things cleverly into the story. 
 What I didn't like: 
 - The constant flash backs to Colin's dating history, such as it was. First of all, I don't consider spending less than an hour with a girl who then decides that she doesn't care about you dating or being dumped, but Colin clearly does. He wallows far too much in the memories of the many Katherines, especially Katherine 19, who seems to have broken his heart. I get that he needs to find "the missing piece of himself", but the umpteenth time it's mentioned, I lose interest 
 - The constant reminders that Hassan is in fact overweight and that Colin has a Jew-fro. I don't think Colin's hair is EVER referred to as just hair - it's always his Jew-fro. I just ran a search for the term and was surprised when it only seems to occur eight times in the whole book. It feels like a LOT more! 
 Most of the book was perfectly inoffensive, but it also didn't grab my interest all that much. If I hadn't been determined that I was going to finish it by the end of February, it would have taken me a lot longer to read than two days, despite the fact that it's not all that long. It had some cute bits, but the supporting cast and some of the nerdy trivia I learned over the course of reading it was better than the general story.

Atlantis Unleashed is the third book in the Warriors of Poseidon series and like its predecessors, it is a light, entertaining read. The story picks up from the cliffhanger from the second book. Justice, one of the Seven warriors sacrificed himself in order to save Ven and Erin. In this story we find Justice trapped in the Void after weeks of torture at the hands of Anubisa, the Vampire Goddess that takes a lickin' and keeps on tickin' (book after book). Half insane, disoriented and hallucinating, he has a vision of a green-eyed, red-haired beauty. He doesn't know who she is, but he knows that she must belong to him. Meanwhile, said beauty, is Dr. Keely McDermott, a feisty archaeologist with an ability to psychically read objects. She gets invited to Atlantis and immediately becomes embroiled in Atlantean affairs when Justice manages to escape from the void. For some reason, the two have a previous connection; hers through a cherished talisman she wears around her neck - an object carved by Justice hundreds of years ago and his from visions experienced while being tortured in the Netherworld. 
 Atlantis Unleashed takes us to from the undersea kingdom of Atlantis to the jungles of South America with battles in ancient ruins, vampire orgies and trips to the past via Keely's object reading ability. The novel contains some scenes that refer to the series wide story arcs but doesn't really require any previous familiarity with the series to understand the context as the characters from past books are only there in minor supporting roles. 
 Throughout Atlantis Unleashed, Lord Justice struggles with the aftermath of his Netherworld experience and dual nature as a Nereid-Atlantean half-breed, which has essentially left him with a split personality whose inner voices want different things from Keely. It remains for Keely to tame his inner demons and help him integrate the personalities.  Even with all of the action and adventure the core of Atlantis Unleashed is about Keely and Justice's romance which is a roller coaster ride as they surmount the obstacles thrown in their way. 
 If you are looking for a fun blend of adventure and paranormal romance you will enjoy Atlantis Unleashed.

 So, I've just marathoned the Adrien English series adn I am in love. 
 In love with Adrien. 
 In love with Jake 
 and in love with Josh Lanyon's writing. 
 I know I'm a decade behind everyone else. I know, okay. The important thing is I've realised the error of my ways and am rectifying the situation by consuming Lanyon's words as quickly as possible. As I didn't review each book of this series separately, I'm going to do one review for books 2-5. I did read 1 ages ago, but was obviously a real doofus who didn't catch on to the beauty of this writing! 
 The thing about this series is the central character Adrien and his, seemingly, doomed love for Jake - the totally in the closet cop. While each book has a fantastic mystery to read and try and solve, it is Adrien and Jake's relationship that kept me hooked and needing to know more. 
 I adored Adrien and his witty observations and curious attitude. I loved Jake and his tough cop persona but together... 
 Oh how I loved their relationship. 
 Even when I hated it. 
 Why? Why did I love it so much? It contained all the things I shouldn't like. A closeted cop. Cheating. Blatant cheating and an off the page woman getting conned into a relationship, a marriage, because Jake hated himself for being gay. 
 I should abhor it. I do, really, in black and white, I would say there is no forgiveness for Jake and Adrien's actions - particularly once Kate was pregnant and Jake had got married. So why was I still devouring it? Wanting more? Desperately wishing Adrien and Jake would have an HEA?? 
 Basically because of Lanyon's writing. He made me see the real people beneath the black and white, right and wrong. 
 Yes, it is wrong to cheat. As civilised human beings we need to consider the feelings of others and not just our own wants and needs. That's not to say we shouldn't pursue what we want but...oh hell, y'all know what I'm saying, right? Cheating is not a nice thing to do. 
 I didn't like Jake for cheating. I didn't like Adrien for being the one Jake cheated with when he knew the situation. 
 And yet I understood it. 
 For all that it was wrong, the fact is, all of the characters in this book were in pain. Jake from the self hatred he carries round - if he can't accept himself as being gay, how will anyone else? To be so despising of your own self...well, I found that the saddest thing of all. I hated that Kate was 'collateral damage' in his fight to come to terms with who he was and who he loved. Well, not who he was, because gay or straight or bi, he was still Jake. He was still the cop. He was still the man the world saw, he just couldn't admit that the man the world saw had fallen in love with another man. 
 It's funny how it was the falling in love that tripped him up. He was happy enough to spend his time in S&M clubs, gay S&M clubs. U=It wasn't the sex, but the feelings, the emotion that he couldn't deal with. 
 Yes his job was partly why he stayed closeted. 
 Yes his family was another part of why he stayed closeted. 
 But really it was only himself who he was hiding from. When he needed the strength to admit what he felt for Adrien. When it literally became life and death, he stepped up tot he mark. 
 Sorry, I didn't mean this to turn into a complete analysis of Jake and his actions!! It obviously struck a chord with me, that even the strongest of people have fears and event he strongest of people hurt those they least want to hurt. We are humans and humans are not perfect and are far from infallible. 
 Lanyon portrays this so well. And he manages to do it while adding humour and mystery to his stories. As I'm probably the last person on the planet to actually read these books, I doubt I have anyone left to recommend them too - but I do, if like me, you've been under a rock. Read these. They're good. 
 (Also, the audio versions are excellent).

This latest entry in John Sandford's Prey series finds BCA detective Lucas Davenport revisiting the first case that took him from uniform to detective in 1985. The mummified bodies of the two missing girls show up under a demolished house 25 years later, and the easy solution to their disappearance, which only Lucas seemed to distrust at the time, is shown to be false. The hunt for the real killer begins. 
 Half of the book is a flashback to the early days of the case. It is a fascinating look at a younger Lucas Davenport, less self-assured and experienced, less wealthy and connected, but still brilliant, brash, ambitious, intuitive and definitely not a team player. The second half of the book takes the case through the new developments as it unfolds. This book would be a fairly good entry to the series, if you have not had the pleasure of Davenport's acquaintance yet. It is a tightly-plotted mystery with interesting characters whose past history deepens but is not critical to enjoyment of the book. As a native Minnesotan, the local color is an added bonus in my eyes. Sandford is one of my favorite mystery writers (although be prepared for a certain amount of mayhem, sometimes unsanctioned and borderline illegal, on the part of the hero in various books throughout the series). A highly recommended mystery, which will make you want to read the rest of the Prey books in order.

After that, the plot, writing and personalities of the characters fall apart (with the exception of Rob because we never got to truly know him as a character up to this point). Seriously, I just felt the book was a mess after the Big Reveal, since Ben finally, finally declares his love for Maddy on the same night they find out her boyfriend cheated on her. And why did he cheat? Because the story called for him to do so, and no other reason. 
 I was somewhat surprised Maddy actually did marry Rob because it was clear to me that at the wedding, and from the Big Reveal onwards that "the one that I want" was Ben. When Maddy forgave Rob and decided to give the relationship another try, it just seemed she did so because of heartbreak over Ben and Alice, and by this point, she had invested five years in Rob, so hey - why not just continue. I think Robert was a habit, and she settled for him, rather than take action to be with the true love of her life, considering how she just could not stop thinking of Ben, or stop yearning for him. [Ben too is fooling himself if he thinks the Kate who makes an appearance at the very end is his true mate.] However, I wasn't very bothered that Maddy did end up with Rob because I felt her romantic feelings for Ben came out of nowhere. Completely, and utterly from zero to "something". Again, plot device. Because there was no build up, it felt totally contrived (unlike with Ben, where we did read about his evolving, years-long love for Maddy). 
 Because too much of the novel felt forced and contrived, I can't recommend the book. OK, maybe read up to the point where Rob confesses he cheated, and then stop reading. Because after that, the novel is just so much tripe.

 "As beautiful as this world is, it's just as dangerous. People who are not useful, people who make mistakes, they can be removed. You can be removed."

I will definitely be recommending this book to anyone I know and I look forward to reading it again in the future.

The Fault in Our Stars aside, John Green is a one-trick pony when it comes to characters and plot. 
 But man, do I like his pony. 
 Yes, Q and Margo are pretty much swappable with Green's other protagonists and their love interests, and the "sidekick" characters are practically the same with just different quirks--but this isn't necessarily a bad thing. Looking for Alaska, An Abundance of Katherines, and Paper Towns felt like a series with similar characters exploring and coming to grips with death, religion, and identity. 
 Paper Towns is certainly the most polished of the three, with Green going off on fewer tangents and only repeating himself when appropriate. Using Whitman as a framework worked better than I had expected it to, and the tone is perfect for young adult. The characters (although recycled) are still fun and fleshed out; my only complaint is that Margo (probably the most interesting) is so absent throughout the novel, and for a novel about identity and finding out who someone really is, it doesn't allow us much room at the end to do so. I think the ending is John Green's best and he handles it beautifully, though, and I'm sure Green would say that the point is the reader only "knows" Margo through the mirrors of the other characters, but it feels like a lost opportunity with a really great character.  
 This is a top-notch YA book that's a fun, quick read for older readers as well. If you aren't a fan of John Green then this certainly isn't a must-read (especially if you've given TFiOS and Looking for Alaska a shot), but if you like him, expect more of the same and enjoy.

 The coordinates to Still Blue have been discovered, and the two factions are scrambling to be the first to get there. But Sable and Hess are holding Cinder, who holds the key to reaching Still Blue. Perry and Aria aren't about to leave Cinder in their custody, even if it means running a suicide mission to get him back. 
 As ends-of-trilogies go, Into the Still Blue was far more thematically consistent and less irritating than, say, Allegiant. Yet it still somehow didn't capture the brilliance of the previous two books, though that's not to say it was bad. Perhaps the most accurate critique I have is that it wasn't what I was expecting. I think I wanted, and would have liked, more of the Still Blue, more of the characters struggling to rebuild, and definitely more description of this place that was only a fable until now. Unfortunately, neither of the two POV characters were heavily involved with the early parts of settling the Still Blue, and once Sable and Hess are defeated, the book is practically over. 
 The early chapters are a bit choppy, probably because Aria and Perry are in the same place and interacting with each other. Thus, in order to capture the thoughts and ideas of both characters, the POV switches, which requires new chapters. When they split up again, the story smooths out and becomes more interesting because each chapter isn't telling us the same thing the last one did. 
 I have every intention of re-reading the trilogy at some point, and it's possible that my rating may go up when I have a chance to read all three books back-to-back instead of spread over a couple of years.

Very fresh story with a great dose of reality. The setting of the Nicaraguan jungles felt so very real, I wasn't at all surprised to learn Amanda Heger had been on a brigade to Nicaragua herself. The descriptions are vivid and so very well written that you really become immersed in the world and culture of the story. 
 This will likely sound odd to say, but I kept finding myself reading with a Latin American/Spanish accent (this was likely helped by the fact that my brother-in-law is from Venezuela). For this reason, I would have preferred the character of Phillip to not be named Phillip since I kept reading it as "Philippe." That's my own fault, of course, haha. :) 
 The sprinkled Spanish throughout the book was generous enough to help bring you into the world, without being too much. I don't know much Spanish, like Annie herself, but I still understood quite a bit of it and literally laughed out loud at this line: 
 "!Es rojo como una bruja! !Una bruja!" 
 Which brings me to the next thing that I liked: the emotions brought up throughout. This story was funny, touching, suspenseful, sad, and sexy. I had gone in expecting more of a romance with a Latin American angle, but was pleasantly surprised to find a story that was focused on Annie and Felipe as people than just as a couple. Most of their relationship is built up in a very natural way, without as many grandiose declarations of "You're The One." As a result of this, it's fairly tame in the steaminess department, but the depth of the bonding otherwise is so enchanting you don't mind. And, rest assured, it's not without some sexiness. Sex itself just isn't the focus. 
 The side characters all added some extra depth and stood on their own without feeling like plot contrivances. Marisol, Phillip and Juan are all great characters. 
 I liked this story and the character development quite a bit. The scene where the woman gives birth - just wonderful. It said so much about the characters and their growth, and made me smile.

Guys! I read a mystery book and I didn't hate it! IT'S A MYRACLE! (I'm really sorry. I just couldn't help myself.) 
 Lots of people have been giving this four or five stars, but before you reach for a copy of "Shine," allow me to say that if you aren't used to reading teen fiction, aren't used to exercising your empathic abilities, or take issue with books in which the characters possess vacillating personalities, this might not be your cup of tea. 
 Here's the deal with Lauren Myracle's work: She is not a witty or "clever" writer. You aren't going to pick up a Lauren Myracle book and start peeling back layers of metaphorical meaning like an artichoke. She doesn't attempt to flatter your ego by paying homage to famous works by famous authors you likely haven't touched since college, and whose ideas you pretend to remember. You are not going to fall in love with any of her characters, or get lost in a fictional universe she's created. Lauren Myracle is not out to pen the next Great American Novel. She is a storyteller working with a pen instead of her voice. She possesses the ability to grab her readers' interest and hold their attention, and it wouldn't matter if she was writing about the apocalypse or last week's grocery list--I guarantee you would be unable to tear your eyes away. 
 This is an excellent pick for reluctant readers. I think anyone who likes Gail Giles, Walter Dean Myers, Patricia McCormick, or John Green would be up for this. It also brought to mind "Thirteen Reasons Why" by Jay Asher, so it might be a good read-alike for that crowd as well.

 This is just another book that suffered under my inability to not compare books. My 3.5 rating doesn't mean I didn't like the story, just that I kept thinking back on how much I liked The Air He Breathes and wanted those same emotions.I also had a few problems with the characters, but nothing too bad that made me hate them. This was still a very beautiful story, that I'm sure affected a lot of people's emotions, but not mine. 
 I loved the connection that Alyssa and Logan had, and that it could survive so much heartache and time apart. Alyssa was actually the character I liked most, which rarely happens because I usually only tolerate the heroines. The strength she showed throughout the story both broke my heart, and put it back together again. She didn't have the hardships that Logan had, yet to me she was the one that had the hardest emotional experience because of her love for Logan. She was his High, but he was her Lo, and she didn't let that break her. 
 My problems mostly came from my own personal issues, and how much I hate reading about addicts. I can sometimes be okay with it if the main character is a recovering addict, but I don't enjoy reading about them while they are still using and having those issues. I couldn't connect with Logan because of his problem in the first half of the book, so I distanced myself from him emotionally. 
 The emotions that I kept waiting to feel, they were sort of there, but not about the main characters. By the end of the book I realized that the only time I was even close to crying didn't even involve Alyssa and Logan together. It made me feel kind of meh that I was more invested in a secondary character than I was about the main ones. 
 Overall, this is a good book that I highly recommend for anyone that likes an emotional read. It was my own issue that lead to me not getting super invested into the characters, and I don't think many others will have that problem.I will definitely be reading this book again some day and maybe then, since it won't be so close to when I read The Air He Breathes, I'll enjoy it more and not compare the two books.

I've been trying to read this for quite a while, but couldn't find the second story anywhere online. Luckily, my lovely boyfriend bought it and lent it to me. 
 Summary of the Story 
 The Search for Sam is the first story and is narrated once again by Adamus, the traitorous Mogadorian. One starts disappearing more often, and she admits they both knew her being with him wasn't going to last forever. He goes back to Ashwood Estates to pretend he is sorry, just so he can access One's body. His father wants to have him killed and allows the new doctor to perform a life threatening operation on him to finally extract One's memories this time. Instead, Adamus knocks out the doctor, and while visiting One in his mind, she transfers her legacy, earthquakes, to him. He collapses the whole building and manages to escape with Sam's dad, the last Greeter alive. 
 Over the next few months, they grow close and help Adamus develop his powers. They go to Paradise so that Malcolm can reconnect with his son at last, but of course, Sam is currently being held captive by the Mogs. The two head to the government compound in New Mexico and end up there at the same time as the rest of the Garde, who are engaging in battle at the other end of the site. 
 They find Sam, and One holds off the Mogs while Sam and his father escape, knowing full well that he will likely die. Accepting this, he uses his legacy to set off the explosives in an attempt to kill everyone at the compound, including himself and his brother, Ivanick.  
 In The Last Days of Lorien, we get a glimpse of Lorien in its final days of existence, from the POV of Sandor, Nine's now deceased cepan. Sandor is a troublemaker who sneaks into clubs by manipulating technology. He is caught by one of his teachers -- but not before meeting his favourite singer, Devektra -- and expelled, forced to either work in the farmlands or attend a school where he will work with technology. He chooses to go to the school, and actually enjoys repairing the grids in the city, even though he notices that almost every one of them is broken. 
 He accompanies a mentor cepan to visit his Garde for the first time. The Garde gives his charge an electronic wristband that matches his own. Sandor sees this as an opportunity to sneak into the city and see Devektra perform again on Lorien's special day of celebration. He borrows the cepan's bracelet as entrance to the club, and visits Devektra backstage. She tells him she has a bad feeling about tonight, but he dismisses it as nerves. 
 During the show, the club is bombed and almost everyone is killed. Sandor receives alerts on his wristband, and is located by Brandon (a.k.a. Henri), the one who recruited him to the school. Brandon is disappointed to find Sandor and not the man the wristband belongs to, as he and his Garde were supposed to be the ninth group to board the ship that will leave Lorien. Sandor travels to the Garde's home and brings him back with him, and Brandon lets him board the ship as well as the Garde's replacement mentor (I'm sure you've figured out by now that the Garde is Nine).  
 In the third and final story, The Forgotten Ones, the POV shifts once again to Adamus, who wakes up among the wreckage of the New Mexico compound, and rescues one of the survived Mogs because he might have information or something. Outside, they run into a wolf, but when Adamus demonstrates his legacy, the wolf is immediately affectionate and protective of him. Even when Dust (what Adamus has decided to name him) transforms from a wolf into a lizard, it still doesn't register with him that Dust is a chimaera. But Rex, the rescued Mog, points it out to him. 
 At first, Rex despises Adamus and plans on turning him in to the Mogs, but after some bonding time admiring Dust and stealing money from a purse thief, they seem to get along. They plan on travelling to another secret Mog compound on an island in New York to rescue the other chimaera that are apparently being held and experimented on. They succeed, but Rex decides to stay behind because although he likes Adamus, he doesn't agree with his beliefs. So Adamus is last seen driving a getaway car full of tiny shape-shifting animals in the back seat. Awesome.  
 What I Thought 
 The Last Days of Lorien was really interesting, and I would love to see a whole book set on Lorien pre-destruction. 
 I was also really glad that the other two books were narrated by Adamus, because, although he is a Mogadorian, he is one of my favourite characters. And I have a theory: What if Adamus is the reincarnation of Pittacus Lore, not any of the Garde? I mean, what if One was originally supposed to be Pittacus (I know she's a girl, but can a girl not be Pittacus?) and she gave him her powers so...or what if Adamus is the only one eventually powerful enough to beat Setrakus Ra because he himself was a Mogadorian and there is something special in that? I don't know, this made more sense in my head, but I think that no matter what, Adamus is going to play a huge role in the Garde's -- hopeful -- defeat over the Mogs, I'm sure.  
 All of the stories were funny and interesting, and everyone knows I love whenever the chimaeras are present in the story. I can't wait to see what Adamus does with a car full of animals, and if he successfully meets up with the other Garde.  
 I guess I'll find out right now, because I'm off to read The Fall of Five!

 I've been wanting to get The Reapers are the Angels by Alden Bell during the time I was so crazy for zombies in fiction, and that's one of the reasons why I got this from Book Depository in the first place. I wanted to add every single book that had zombies in it, until it became a little bit too mainstream for my taste. That's probably why I made this book languish in my TBR for a while, almost forgetting that I had this book with me until lately. Because you know, sometimes you have to dig through your TBR just to get some books out and get that number down. 
 The Reapers are the Angels introduces a world that is full of zombies. There's nothing really new about that, but then here comes Temple, a fifteen year old girl who's turned herself into a vagabond after something happened in her past. She runs into a small community of survivors who take her in, but when she accidentally kills a man who tried to take advantage of her, she is back on the run now that his brother is after her. On her journey, she meets a group of hunters who take on a new way of survival, picks up a mentally challenged man who becomes her unwanted ward, stays with a rich family who refuses to acknowledge the state of the world and gets caught by a horrifically mutated group of people whose loyalty to each other leads them to kill. All this time, Temple fights the evil she thinks is in her while running away from the man who wants to kill her. 
 Or perhaps running away isn't the right term. As the story goes on, it doesn't really feel that Temple was running away -- perhaps there was something else. It was almost like this chase gave her some kind of purpose, and it was interesting to read about that. Temple is a different girl and we know it right from the start. Why she chose to be alone is a mystery, and how she seemed to unafraid later on as she travels is another question. Her character makes this initially simple and typical zombie story come more alive. The Reapers are the Angels isn't a story of zombies or the fallen world but a story of a person wrestling with her past and trying to atone for this. Temple's brokenness makes her who she is -- the hard, no-nonsense girl with awesome fighting skills -- but it doesn't lessen her compassion for others who need her help, even if she doesn't really want to help at all. I found her unlikely "friendship" with Maury, the mentally challenged guy she helps and "adopts", quite endearing and possibly my favorite part in the entire story.  
 But this book isn't really an easy read. The lush writing helped a lot in making me want to read this, but this is a bleak book -- not quite as hopeless as The Forest of Hands and Teeth and also not quite as action packed as The Enemy, but still pretty, well, not cheerful. There were also lots of philosophical talk, which makes this book really a story of survival and how humanity carries on after an apocalypse. I think what makes this book a little harder for me to read was the gross-out factor -- like I said, I may have gone soft, and there were some scenes in this book that made me stop reading for a bit just so my stomach would stop churning. Oh Tina, what do you expect of a zombie book, anyway? Just...don't read this while eating, especially for some parts. 
 Even so, I find that I loved The Reapers are the Angels, especially for how it ended. Sigh. --> That will be my one and only clue for you. I think The Reapers are the Angels is a beautifully sad but deep book, and I was a very satisfied reader when I finished the book. It's not at the level of how much I loved Mira Grant's Feed, my favorite zombie book of all time, but Alden Bell's creation has made it into the list of zombie books I will recommend to people who want to read about them. This is a good one, folks -- gross scenes aside, this is a zombie book that lived up to my expectations, and I hope it lives up to yours, too.

 I loved Kady as our main protagonist (having pink hair - hell yeah!), especially the way she started the story off... by breaking up with Ezra . I've never experienced a character do that so early on. She's a hacker, and we don't have enough protagonists like that (a lot of them are good archers of swordsmen/women haha)! I loved how the authors wrote about her knowledge of coding and IT - it was slightly confusing to deeply understand, but nevertheless fun to read. 
 And that seriously makes me want to point out the unique style in which the book was written, not to mention its fantabulous book cover (I usually never buy a book for its cover, but this one...yeah) 
 I loved the IMs, the emails, and other messages - it made the book such a fast-paced read, just like the plot itself! 
 The detail of each battle scene, notably  the Kerenza IV attack, the first and second Lincoln attack  took my breath away! Kaufman and Kristoff do an amazing job at describing something so intense in an unconventional form. 
 One thing that I found realistic in the novel, which was a plus for me, was the time spacing of all the events. It made sense to me that  Kady and Ezra would basically be fighting to no end after they've broken up while their planet is invaded. It makes sense that they stay broken up for about seven months before making up and getting back together. Because, in reality, no one breaks up and gets back together right away (but some books do manage to do that still...)  
 One of my favourite things about Illuminae was the premise of the plot itself. Conspiracy. Invasion. Terrorist attacks. Artificial Intelligence. Finding and taking out the real villain. It was done in an original way - so thumbs up to that! 
 Things that were unexpected: 
 1.  Kady's mom was dead? She was on the Copernicus the whole time? Now it makes sense why she avoided talking about her with Ezra on the IMs. And since I wasn't sure, I went back to the pages listing the Copernicus casualties - and there was Kady's mom (alongside the names of Leigh Bardugo, Amie Kaufman, and Jay Kristoff....hmmm)  
 2.  AIDAN's bitchiness - yeah, that's right. He was a son a * most of the book, and I disliked reading from his p.o.v. so much (seconded only by Alexander's ex-commander Torrence...a-hole). I WAS SITTING ON THE BUS WITH MY MOUTH OPEN AT THE PART WHERE AIDAN TRICKED KADY TO COME TO THE ALEXANDER AND TOLD HER EZRA WAS DEAD. I was literally thinking for over a hundred pages "he can't be dead, he can't be dead, no, no, no, OMFG  
 3.  Ok, ok, this may come as a shock, but I wasn't expecting the whole Phobos virus released by BeiTech thing. I thought we were going to focus on some hidden reason behind why they attacked Kerenza and made AIDAN go berserk and kill everyone on Copernicus. The scene with Zhang and Mcnulty on the Alexander scared me to death because, what's worse than zombies? PTSD zombies in space, apparently!  
 4.  The fact that Ezra's mom is the head of BeiTech and commandeered the attack on Kerenza and is the villain who stared this mess? Wow, what a villain (sorry AIDAN, you become a semi-nice guy to Kady by the end) - but she still gets her ass kicked by the Illuminae Group (i.e. Katy and her gang)  
 5.  Which includes...Ezra! He's alive. That son of a * AI tricked everyone, but mostly Kady. It was the best thing ever to see their reunion after not having seen each other for more than half a year.  That scene was a spectacular job on Kaufman and Kristoff's part! Because I seriously thought that  Kady was going to die alongside AIDAN (who doesn't really end up dead - since he's a computer) and the Alexander...like I was getting R&J and Titanic vibes - but the Aussie authors listened to my prayers. YES!  
 My favourite part of the book was surprisingly the whole chunk of black pages toward the end, which was nice because I didn't like  AIDAN's  p.o.v. in the beginning - but I really enjoyed it then! 
 I will try my best to wait patiently for Book 2 :)

 And while I love Sophie as a character (especially how she adapts with aplomb to instantly becoming "a hale old woman"), I just can't warm up to Howl. I kept thinking I'd rather be reading about Christopher Chant or The Ogre Downstairs . 
 It's how I felt when the book first came out, and derned if it isn't how I still feel rereading it thirty years later.

The shiny key on the cover, and the interesting teaser blurb in the dust jacket made it seem like it had so much promise. Unfortunately, the disjointed plot, and atrophied support cast and plots, are just making me file this right next to Hunger Games. (Although Hunger Games would be pretty close to this book if it frequently alternated between Katniss' and Haymitch's points of view.) 
 I will not be reading the sequel.

The writing style is rather difficult to get used to and the constantly crossed out lines annoyed me to no end at first. In the end it was the book's atmosphere that made me fall for it. It's interesting that The Haunted Mask directly follows The Ghost Next Door in the Goosebumps series. Rather than a book of monsters or witches, both are more psychological in nature. But where the Ghost Next Door failed to go deep into the mind of the main character, the Haunted Mask is actually a pretty decent thriller. 
 In the story, Carly Beth is the most easily scared kid in school. And he friends love nothing more than doing just this. But this Halloween, Carly Beth is going to turn the table. So she buys the scariest, most realistic mask she can find (despite the hesitations of the shopkeeper). 
 As the story continues, we get a very close look at the danger of the mask. It changes her voice, makes her violent and angry, and eventually connects itself to Carly Beth. Where the Ghost Next Door didn't go too in depth, in that Haunted Mask, we get a great look at the slow transition from nice young girl to violent monster. 
 My only issue (and it is a common issue with Goosebumps books) is that there is too much focus on the main character. Interesting characters are often glossed over. Like the scientist in Say Cheese and Die, I would love to know more about the shopkeeper. Why did he make the masks? Why did he make the masks? How did he bring them to life? And because of these questions, it gets a similar ranking to Say Cheese and Die. 
 1. Night of the Living Dummy 
 2. Say Cheese and Die 
 3. Welcome to Dead House 
 4. The Haunted Mask 
 5. Welcome to Camp Nightmare 
 6. Stay Out of the Basement 
 7. Monster Blood 
 8. The Ghost Next Door 
 9. The Curse of the Mummy's Tomb 
 10. Let's Get Invisible 
 11. The Girl Who Cried Monster

This story is thoroughly engaging and wonderfully scripted, incorporating a vibrant BDSM world with fantasy elements. The characters are interesting and captivating and the sexual aspects of the world pale in comparison to the mystery and world building dynamics. Although the world building and characters had problems, the darker edge will entice readers and those who enjoy fantasy mixed with BDSM won't be able to put this book down. 
 As the blurb suggests, the story is about a house slave Tam who helps a Lucan, a mage, solve the mystery of who is attacking the wealthy and protected guild. Lucan is hired to investigate discretely, often using Tam to help navigate the city. Tam is essential in helping Lucan with the final resolution, but that may not mean much in the world when slaves are insignificant. 
 The story is told in first person from Tam's point of view and is well written and complex, incorporating numerous elements and ideas almost seamlessly. The world building is really stunning with the complicated characters yet the strength of the writing shines in the use of magic and recognizable social structure. At the same time, this is one of the major problems with the book. Although the world building is really the best part, simultaneously the world created is too easy. There are very low levels of conflict, if any, within the world and the mystery is the main source of tension in a strictly regulated and harshly run world. The concept and execution of the guilds mean that the kind of destruction and chaos created is almost never heard of and thus, the unusual mystery. 
 At the same time, there is no abuse of the rules, no rebellion and angst among the slaves. This world is one where technology seems to be absent or at least rudimentary and the slaves are used for everything from message running to cart pulling. Slaves themselves are not bitter, angry, and resentful for their lot in life. Conversely, they accept their beatings as due course and consider their life as lucky for the most part. Even though the Free express their affection with slaps, hits, and the occasional thrown food, slaves fall upon this happily and eagerly. This world is intricate and interesting but skirts the line of too accepting and easy. It's difficult to add complexity and tension in a world where no one abuses slaves, slaves understand and accept beatings almost with a smile, and there is no jealousy or animosity among slaves. 
 This ease of life is likely created on purpose to offset the darkness of the D/s world where the edgy dynamic could overwhelm the story and turn the reader away. Since Tam has no issues with his treatment, the reader is lured into the same complicity and acceptance. Tam's easy and complete acquiescence of his status, life and treatment is essential to his character. His personality shows hints of intelligence, independence, and wit and these spark with vibrancy when shown against the backdrop of almost blind obedience. Tam is a strong character and craves the domination of his Master while clearly possessing an intelligence and skill set well above the menial and inconsequential tasks of a house slave. I do wish he had shown his personality more as his one, incredibly short lived sulking against his unfair whipping was anemic and showed more weakness of character than strength. If he'd shown more tension and drama for not only that beating but his growing emotional connection to Lucan, this would have added depth to the character. 
 Either way, Tam is a compelling narrator and creates a dark atmosphere and world with evocative phrases and prose. His views of those around him, specifically Lucan tantalite and show true mastery in almost casual cruelty. This bland acceptance of slaves' obedience and therefore station sparks with tension only intermittently when hints of more depth to Lucan are shown. If these hints remain true, a sequel could delve more intimately into the D/s dynamics of Tam and Lucan and their emotional connection. 
 Let me say even with the problems I've noted, this is a wonderful story. The prose is engaging and the author's voice as told in first person through Tam is instantly captivating. Especially wonderful is the trip to Hell and the scene of Lucan with the dead bodies. The world building and characters draw the reader in immediately and carry the journey to the end, leaving hope for a sequel. This book lacks the lyrical eloquence of the author's other work but instead delivers a story full of dark energy and creative interest. I eagerly await a sequel and easily recommend this book to those readers who enjoy BDSM themes and darker fantasy stories. Don't worry though, there is a happy ending.

Murder mystery meets James Bond (without the secret agents). 
 What do I mean by this? 
 Murder mystery because, well, 3/4 of the book is shaped around solving a murder. There are twists, turns, police action, citizens-turned-detective, etc. If you can suspend your annoyance with the author for deliberately misleading you enjoy the ride, it can be a real page-turner. 
 James Bond because there is a lot of sleuthing, happy coincidences, and plenty of casual sex between smart, beautiful, flat characters. The good guys are all about the same; they talk the same, have the same values, and while they may be occasionally mistaken, they never do anything evil. The bad guys are bad. Lisbeth Salander, the main character, is pretty interesting, but most of the other characters blur together. 
 Page-turning ability: starts out at a 5 or 6 (sort of slow, but not too bad) and picks up to a 7 or so about 1/4 of the way through. About 3/4 of the way through it's up to an 8 or 9 (hard to put down). 
 Literary greatness: not much. Flat characters, straight-forward writing, and an interesting plot. 
 Child-appropriateness: none. There is tons of sex, none of it between married people. It's also depressing, casual, uncommitted sex. There's also some pretty graphic violence. 
 All in all, I would have given it 4 stars except for the unnecessary and pervasive un-committed sex. Because that bothers me, I drop it to 3 stars.

first of all, this book is not about vampires who love each other accross centuries. Phew. It's about reincarnated people who love each other across centuries... And maybe the devil. 
 It would have been a lot better if it had been about 150 pages shorter. I can enjoy the "girl falls for guy, she finds out he might be hiding something and may possibly be evil, she becomes disillusioned with their love and hates him and vows to leave him, she finds out she was wrong and that he was always awesome, she swoons for him all over again" plot line like anyone else. But it has to happen just like that, ONE TIME. The girl can't be constantly discovering evil things about her lover and running away from him and then forgiving him two pages later only to find more evil things about him in the next chapter, repeat ad nauseum! 
 Granted, I didn't expect this to be a stellar book. But it achieved it's purpose: to entertain me while I got over the end of my cold.

So.. I don't know why I took such a long time getting around to this series! Geez, maybe because the description sounds cheesy/lame (bird-people, seriously?) but I was pleasantly surprised. This action/adventure story is fast-paced with great characters, coupled with an interesting mystery and clever plot. Patterson really thought this out, because these scientific things seem mildly possible and believable. 
 What did I like the most? The characters, hands down. Max isn't necessarily "amazingly deep, complex, and 3-D" but she's an admirable heroine who is determined to protect her family. She cares for the younger ones, acting as a natural leader, comforter, and even a mother at times. The younger kids trust her inexplicably, probably because she has pulled through for them so many times. Her narration throughout the majority of the book was well-written IMO, because she did 'speak' about her worries, fears, and honest thoughts, not just 'narrating a story'. I liked Fang's character, and how delicious he sounds (licks lips in a non-creepy manner) but he was a bit flat. Maybe it was because he never said much, but I just didn't get much personality vibe from him, apart from the fact that he cared deeply for Max and the other kids. 
 I liked how even though Patterson had 6+ main characters, he didn't let any of them get pushed aside. Fang, Iggy, Gasman, Nudge, and Angel all get developed decently enough, and are big parts of the novel, not just some minor person. I liked the way the 6 of them always stuck together like a family, but still bickered and whatnot. The antagonists were interesting as well, and they made good bad-guys, if you get what I say. Unique but deadly. 
 Another thing I liked was the 'scientific' aspect of the novel, with the DNA modifications, mutations, and the different 'creatures' created. The Erasers are an interesting concept, with them managing to evolve from a handsome model-person to a snarling wolf. The flying may sound cheesy, but Patterson seems to pull it off and make it seem 'cool'. The different powers the kids develop are also unique, but I won't spoil it for you. Just know that I'm pretty jealous :P 
 4/5 - because I severely underestimated it. I didn't think I would like it, and I'm really happy to be proven wrong. I was so caught up in the story, and loved the plot and characters (a lot!). I liked the 'mutants' (which seems like a cruel way to put it) that Patterson created, and really enjoyed the non-stop action. Don't judge the book by it's cover (lame cover, IMO) or its description (also lame IMO), I just advise you to try it. Recommend to people who want to read a fast-paced action/adventure novel with a cool plot and interesting characters with cool abilities. Pretty guy-friendly as well, I think.

This book was hilarious. It was such a fun and interesting read- and it's a kind of book that I've never come across so far. It's adult. It's comedy. It's fantasy. It's dark. It's dramatic. I didn't even know a book like this existed! 
 Charlie's wife, Rachel, who he absolutely adores and loves, dies tragically after his daughter is born. He unfortunately sees a mint green man take a prized CD of his wife. But he isn't supposed to see the mint green dressed man! So then he becomes a death merchant. and his daughter becomes Death, with a capital D.  This means he has to collect the souls of people who die or are about to die. I don't know what else I can say about this book. 
 It's just funny. The plot isn't great. The characters are pretty flat- but this book is funny. And it pretty much does a great job at being funny.

Suspense: 
 I read about 30% of the book at which point I figured out the ending. Then I read till 40% mark and lost all interest because all indications pointed to that ending. 
 Writing style: 
 I dragged myself for yet a couple more pages but the story was progressing at snail's pace. I felt the author digresses from the point way too much. For ex. when the protagonist is taking a drive then he describes the farm that's passing by, who owns that farm, what are the owners hobbies, who are his guests, what artists do and finally comes back to Natalie - what she did as an artist. You get the idea. There's way too much of unneeded detail. I was literally skipping a couple of paragraphs and reading a few lines, again skipping a few paras then reading again without losing any info. 
 Story: 
 The story sounded really interesting when I started reading it. However the plot progresses a bit slow. There's a lot of action happening but that's not really what I want. I want the character to ask important questions, do the first things first but he doesn't do them. For ex.  When two people try to kidnap him in college one of them hits Barry. Clearly Barry must have seen that guy. So later on when they're discussing about how there's no trace of those two people the most sensible thing would be to meet up with Barry, ask him whether he saw those two people, is he okay, what's his verion of the story. But instead the main character ignores him completely.  
 Then there are weird character personas. For ex the FBI turned teacher friend he has. What happens is  she agrees to trace Natalie for him. Then later meets him and her update is that she found nothing. But instead of telling it to him like a normal person she starts asking him lots of personal questions. I found that really weird. It doesn't fit in with a character. If you had no info for someone what would you do? You would just tell them that you have no info. But instead if you were asking them detailed qs it meant that you had some kind of hypothesis in your head that you were trying to work out. It's just a weird character. And then both of them don't communicate with each other which was again a weird thing. Are they normal people or do they have some kind of trust disorder?  
 Overall: 
 It sucked. Bad characters. Lot of action but no noticeable progress in plot. Lots of - yeah, yeah, uh-huh, but little concrete conversation. People around acting weird for no reason. Sucked! I'm glad I'm able to drop books without any guilt. There are millions of books coming out every year and I would much rather spend time reading something that I connect with.

There are a few loose ends I kind of wish were tightened a bit more and a few times I had to take a minute to remember what was happening in Autumn and Summer's storylines (I mixed them up a couple of times and I kept forgetting which one was Trey's daughter and which was the other guy's daughter). But I have to say I don't like that Autumn lives with Marie and the rest at the end?? (The news article says that all 5 of Kristina's children now live with Marie.) She and her grandfather don't have the world's warmest relationship, but they DO love each other and she effectively abandons him alone in Texas?? On Christmas?? After she explicitly tells him that she'll come back to him?? Wth Autumn?? And what was with that rape apologist bull at the end with Hunter?????????

I had to stop reading this because Nora was such an ineffectual protagonist I couldn't care about her or the stupid decisions she was making. The title lead me to believe it would be a smart woman thrown into a world with magic, not a bumbling woman incapable of making a decision to save her life. Reading a couple other reviews, I think I made the right choice in not wasting more of my life reading this. The writing was all right but the characters were all flat (and apparently don't get any more fleshed out) and the plot failed to snare my attention in any way.

Reviewed by: Rabid Reads 
 I was super excited when I first discovered this novel because I've been meaning to give Kristen Painter's writing a try, and although I've heard great things about her HOUSE OF COMARRE series, I have a more difficult time playing catch-up than I do jumping on the bandwagon at book 1. HOUSE OF THE RISING SUN has a lot going for it including captivating characters, detailed world-building, and a strong plot. Overall, I thought it was a good first installment, and a great introduction to Painter's new CRESCENT CITY universe. However, I did have a major issue with Harlow; I found her to be very self-absorbed and I couldn't sympathize with her daddy issues. She does get better as the story progresses, and I'm all for character growth, but her brattiness was just too extreme that it was difficult to see past it. 
 I really loved the world-building in this first installment--I wish there had been more of it! The CRESCENT CITY universe is so rich and diverse that I was hoping for a background chapter or maybe a glossary to help fill-in some of the blanks. Now, it's my understanding that Augustine's a secondary character from this author's first series, so I'm assuming I would have probably benefited from starting with HOUSE OF COMARRE. But, already I find myself fascinated by all of the different types of fae. What sets the Shadeux apart from the Smokesinger and the Raptor? Vampires, shifters, witches, and voodoo further complete the picture, and help ensure that all paranormal readers will be able to enjoy this book no matter their preferred poison. 
 Harlow. Where do I begin? She and I did not get off to a good start. I found her bratty and very self-absorbed, and my opinion of her didn't change until well past the mid-way point. I struggled to understand why she chose to alienate herself from her mother because of a man (her dad) she never met. Her attitude towards her inheritance on the tail end of her mother's death was distasteful, and her prejudice against the fae was unjustified, especially given her genetics. Harlow does eventually begin to grow, and I found myself liking the character she might one day become if she continues down her new path. Unfortunately, the author made her heroine a little too hateful to the point that Harlow's behaviour actually overshadowed some of this novel's other merits. 
 Augustine is a phenomenal character, and I can definitely understand why he earned his own spin-off series. I liked how his dark and light sides battle each other; he wants to do right by Olivia, his mom and Harlow, but it's so hard to please everyone, and revenge has a way of twisting even the best of intentions. I enjoyed the diversity and scope of Painter's secondary characters; Dulcinea, Fenton and Lally were insta-favourites, and I look forward to learning more about their backgrounds and seeing what roles they will play as this series progresses. It's also worth mentioning that the villain is especially heinous, and I'm optimistic that the hunt is going to be almost as satisfying as the eventual final showdown. 
 New Orleans is a great setting for this story, and the author makes good use of her location. I enjoyed the beginnings of Kristen Painter's main plot arc, and see a lot of potential for future installments. HOUSE OF THE RISING SUN has one major downfall, but otherwise delivers on all fronts. I have high hopes for CITY OF ETERNAL NIGHT.

 These books in this series fascinate, impress, and transfix me with the situations, storyline and predicaments these guys and gals find themselves in. 
 Rock Babineaux is an "enigma wrapped in a riddle and surrounded by bearded stubble". Yep, that describes him perfectly. I loved Rock. Dame he was hot, sexy, and protective. Vanessa Cordova, hired as a communication specialist for the Black Knights. I liked her. She is strong, determined, and pushes herself past her limited experiences to bring back Rock. These two work well together. The sexual tension was just oozing off the pages. The action and suspense kept me transfixed and glued to the pages. I love the additional side characters and of course the previous characters. It all adds a great dynamic to the book, especially when you add in the banter and humor they have. It shows you how close everyone is. How the Black Knights have become a family. 
 I love the Black Knights Inc. series. The characters and situations are always entreating. Thrill Ride delivers an action packed adventure! If you have not picked up this series yet, I highly recommend you do.

An amazing story about a girl sentanced to death for killing a man who's father took her in off the street and clothed and fed her. 
 In a world where there are no excuses to crimes and punishment is set in stone Yelena is offered an oppurtunity for life, a life where she is constatly in danger of dying. 
 People are not what they seem and its hard to know who you can trust so is it worth it? 
 I was pulled into Yelenas story and followed her journey through her training and discoveries and found this book very hard to put down. 
 Yelena is a mere girl when a torturous life forces her to commit the sin of murder. The book opens with Yelena in the dungeon, she's been there almost a year. She is to hang for her crimes and confesses, she did kill him. Now comes an incredible choice, face the gallows and die now or take a job as the Commanders food tester, never sure when you may die from an assasination attempt. Yelena has more than just poisons to worry about though as the father of the man she killed tries to have her killed and with more enemies then friends, its very hard for Yelena to know who to trust and there is a reason since everyone seems keen on ending her life.
that was one hell of a romp

"In Cassiel's name, I protect and serve" 
 Many have reservations about this book. There is certainly a fair amount of erotica, but don't let that fool you. The intricacy of this book's plot provokes emotions that make people look at me strange if I'm reading it in a public place. 
 The first part of the book is your basic "how the character was raised" fantasy introduction. But the feelings come in waves once Joscelin Verreuil enters the story. And it builds and builds as they go through a terrible journey together. So I've provided my emotional reaction to a specific scene in the book. I've hidden the details as spoilers, and left the emotions readily available for your reading pleasure. 
 At the battle of Troyes-le-Mont , Phedre no Delauney picked her way across the enemy encampment, as they held siege, in order to deliver a message to her queen. I see this in my mind over and over again. I see her dangerously delivering her message to the guards in the fortress. I see Waldemir Selig catch her and drag her to her knees. I hear him yelling at the fortress, telling the queen to watch how he pleases spies. I see him rip off her dress and bring the knife to her flesh and start to skin her alive. And then  I hear her scream. Gods how I hear her scream, so loud that it reaches into the heart of the fortress and the heart of my soul. It rings over and over in my mind. I see the red haze of pain and hear the beating of Kushiel's wings. I see Joscelin ride up, madness in his eyes, and I hear him challenge Selig to the Holmgang and then, after, in order to save the woman he's oathsworn to protect. I see him take his daggers out, one poised to throw into Phedre's heart and the other ready to slit his own throat,  and then I hear it. "In Cassiel's name, I protect and serve." And I cry. I go back and reread the passage and I put the book down and replay it over and over in my head for years. And when the memory starts to fade, I pick the book up again. No passage in any book has ever touched me the way the beginning of the battle of Troyes-le-Mont has.

What a lovely story of friendship and family and people trying to find how they fit in the world when the force that has previously shaped their lives is yanked away. In the case of Sydney, that force is her brother-- Peyton has always been the golden child, but when he embarks on a destructive path as a teen, it culminates in his severely injuring a bike rider and ultimately serving time in jail. While he is incarcerated, his shadow still falls over Sydney and her relationship with her parents. She leaves the private school where she will be forever judged as his little sister, and starts at Jackson High School. As she comes into her own with a new circle of friends, Sydney's overprotective mother cannot see beyond her fear that her daughter may choose the same destructive lifestyle that her son did, despite all evidence to the contrary. Dessen does relationships beautifully, and each of the characters-- primary and secondary-- grow in utterly believable and satisfying ways. 
 One of my favorite passages: 
 "You never knew what lay ahead; the future was one thing that could never be broken, because it had not yet had the chance to be anything. One minute you're walking through a dark woods alone, and then the landscape shifts, and you see it. Something wondrous and unexpected, almost magical, that you never would have found had you not kept going." 
 Sydney faces many of those dark passages, and it's not always clear whether she will come out on the other side, discovering that wondrous bit of herself.

Spoilers throughout- be warned!  
 I wrote in my review of Divergent that the trains represent the book itself: evocative, vivid, continuous fast-paced action, making up for an irrational premise (trains that never charge a fare and never stop running and never stop at a station? Who pays for the fuel, and why don't the other factions insist that the trains stop at stations so they can be a public service usable by factions other than the Dauntless?) 
 Insurgent loses that fast-paced flow of action, so there's less distraction from the irrationalities of the story. The book opens with Tris having just been shot. Losing a great deal of blood apparently has no effect on her ability to function, because being tough means that physiology is only for other people. 
 When people are shot and and bleed profusely, besides watching the murder of their parents, in addition to killing their own close friend, amidst the slaughter of nearly all their childhood friends at the hands of their new friends due to mass deployment of a mind control serum by an enemy faction, in an event which signals a catastrophic breakdown of the five-faction society they have always known and may well render them factionless in the wake of a regime change within their own faction, they will go into shock. That is what will happen to the body after the adrenaline crashes. If it does not happen and the character functions pretty normally, jumping on and off of trains and following the proceedings of a journey and a group discussion with interest and connectedness, it is not a sign of toughness. It is a sign that what you are struggling to read is not very authentic. 
 Going back to my earlier train analogy, the train does not shoot on an exciting ride through a vivid cityscape in this book. It putters to a halt and sits and thinks about its boyfriend for ages, then fights with the boyfriend, demands the truth from the boyfriend, and lies to the boyfriend. They make up and make out, and the train sporadically starts chugging again until it peters out for the next go-round. 
 This has stopped being about a girl fighting for her place in the world and for her friends' safety and for the greater good of their society, who also has a special romance on the side. It started being about a girl who loves her boyfriend and is mad at him and wants the truth but tells a lie and loves him soooo much, plus there's other stuff going on. 
 I hoped that some of the plot problems would be skillfully explained in Insurgent. Actually the big explanation turned out to be even less internally consistent or rational. An eyerolling cliffhanger ending that was intended to be shocking revealed that the faction system was very recently thought up and then implemented through some kind of brainwashing. No word on why they think you cannot be both clever and brave, but it seems that they predicted that if you make up a nonsensical faction system of non-mutually exclusive personality traits and truly believe that they are mutually exclusive, then people with special brains would "evolve" and save humanity. No word on how the saving would happen, but it's important to cause the factions to think that the ones who can save us are a dangerous threat who should be eliminated. 
  
 My vote: don't bother to read Insurgent unless you feel addicted to Divergent. The fast-paced action is gone, and the characters are different and somehow less compelling.

The premise of "The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas" is a time-honored one: is the happiness of an entire civilization worth the suffering of just one person? The question has been posed in many forms over the years, but Ursula K. Le Guin poses it again in this short story about a seemingly utopian society that ends up being more like a well-hidden dystopia, with its dark secret tucked away in a cellar somewhere. Except the thing is that it's not a secret: everyone knows the sacrifice the town of Omelas has given so everyone else can have happiness, the simple yet not-so-simple form they all wish to achieve. Le Guin's story is a description of the town and its shortcomings, an interesting read, especially thinking about the what-ifs and all the questions that are raised about how such a society came to be and why people still believe what they do to maintain their way of life. Is it worth it to turn a blind eye to suffering and continue to live in isolation and denial? Is it better to escape Omelas, to accept reality and to realize that life is nuanced and has as many good and bad aspects as their are grains of sand on this earth? This is not my favorite short story by any means, but certainly one worth reading. The link to read it online is here.

I think Mary Calmes is a guilty pleasure. I read her books and can point out the flaws, of which there are many, yet there is an engaging voice and sheer outrageousness to the characters and actions that delivers an entertaining and fun read regardless. Calmes is the kind of reader that fans love even if the story has issues and I can appreciate that because there is something about the characters that draws you in. I easily read Trusted Bond in one sitting and although it sets up the same situation over and over again - Jin in trouble, again as everyone wants him - the story remains entertaining. 
 In this sequel to Change of Heart, Jin and his mate Logan are back. Jin is the star of this story as his special status makes him a repeated target. I'd suggest you read the first book before tackling the sequel or re-read the first book if you want to understand it all. You can pick this one up for the sheer guilty pleasure and not care about the various interconnecting storylines and then it won't matter. I'd read CoH over a year ago and while I could remember some details, Trusted Bond throws out tons of names, details, positions, and situations that seem foreign without any context. I was pretty lost in how the majority of these people and their jobs/positions connected to Jin and his family but after a while I just gave up and didn't care. 
 The world building feeds into this confusion since it's so haphazard. The rules and theories of the werepanther world change to meet whatever tension and drama is needed. This is what happened in the first book and continues here with rules mentioned and then ignored later with no consequences. It keeps the tension high as the overly political were packs have tons of rules, regulations, laws, and protocol that all work to keep Jin from Logan, or so it seems. So the reader is never quite sure what will happen since really anything can. It's a very sloppy way of creating tension with messy world building at best. Additionally, many of the characters offer information via dialogue that makes no sense. The information is important for the reader but the characters would already know it, so their saying it is a clumsy way of conveying that information to the reader. 
 The action tends to be very frantic and exaggerated with the characters even more so. Jin is once again the special were panther with abilities never seen in one like him before. He's the super special flower, the only one in existence that's like him and well if you've read Calmes books before you know how exaggerated and perfect her characters tend to be. Jin is no better but he has warmth and charm that makes you want to forgive his obvious characterization and root for him anyway. His chemistry with Logan is smoking hot and their sex scenes are delightful, sexy, and plentiful. He is too perfect though and he only becomes more so in this book with even more power, even more special abilities, and even more people vying to save or kill him. 
 The frantic action keeps the story hopping though as Jin manages to be beaten, kidnapped, and/or both no less than three times in a row. There is some relationship drama with Logan as Logan's gay for you love freaks Jin out. Jin comes to put more trust and faith in Logan and their love by the end of the story and the two have a special, one of a kind connection. Their relationship works even though Logan never really gets out of his rather flat, two dimensional box. The story is all about Jin though so that's ok. I wish Domin and Koren would get their own book because that's a couple that nearly steals all the attention when they're on page. 
 Really the engaging writing and easy to read entertainment make this a fun guilty pleasure. It has a lot of problems though so for those readers that are bothered by messy world building, clumsy information dumps, perfect characters, and obvious scenarios may have problems with this. It's not perfect at all and will appeal more to those readers that can ignore the faults because they enjoy the writing anyway. If you're that reader - you'll likely adore this. If you're not, I wouldn't recommend this.

There are some books that are good. There are some books that are great and every once in a while there's a book that's phenomenal. The Beginning of Everything was phenomenal. This book is just about as brutally honest as coming of age stories go. The Beginning of Everything represents life, teenage angst, first loves, and first heartbreaks. It represents what it means to find yourself in the most unlikely of times and around the most unlikeliest of people. The book represents what it means to grow up and face shattered dreams and later a hopeful future. The Beginning of Everything was a clear representation of what it means to be a teenager today. 
 I feel like reading this book was a privilege in itself. It's rare to find a YA contemporary that truly speaks to you, that you connect with a hundred percent and the book itself feels like an extension of your own body, especially told from an honest male's POV. But that's just what The Beginning of Everything was; it was honest and rare, raw and funny. It tore my heart out into a million pieces and threaded it back together by the end. Our injured protagonist, Ezra is one of my favorite characters of all time. He was intelligent and funny, his constant witty remarks had me smiling and laughing out loud. There were moments I had to close the book, tip my head back and have a nice giggle at the things he thought. Ezra really grows into himself in the book, he matures and realizes just how vain and selfish he used to be and not only realizes it but he even gets disgusted by it. We see how the events after the accident really put things in perspective for Ezra and how he comes to accept his past and look into the future with open arms. Ezra even went out of his way to make sure he'd never be the old vain and childish self he once was, he was repulsed by how he used to be and knew he didn't want to go there again. 
 The romance in this book I also found to be really enjoyable. It was slow building, not perfect and exactly the way teenage romance really is. The relationship between Cassidy and Ezra wasn't without its faults, they weren't perfect and that's just what made them all the more memorable. They had their fair share of bumps in the road and nothing was ever really simple with the two. This book is Ezra's story about finding himself and his belief that Cassidy was the catalyst to his new life, to him changing his ways all the while Ezra may not have been Cassidy's. I love how Robyn Schneider left things with Ezra and Cassidy in the book, it went along with my own beliefs that sometimes a person can change your life, but that doesn't mean you're the one to change theirs. 
 "I still think that everyone's life, no matter how unremarkable, has a singular tragic encounter after which everything that really matters will happen. That moment is the catalyst--the first step in the equation. But knowing the first step will get you nowhere--it's what comes after that determines the result. -- Robyn Schneider, The Beginning of Everything 
 The Beginning of Everything deals with the belief of tragedy, and how one's true honest self is born from tragedy. The book explores how one only truly accepts life and learns the meaning of living it to the fullest after tragedy strikes. This belief is what really struck a chord in me and I was able to connect with it from the start. I have yet to go through my own personal tragedy, and in all honesty I'm scared to death too. But this theory Ezra has is one I've had myself for years, years and years of watching drama movies and drama reading books have left me with the idea that maybe I won't know how to fully live life until after I've nearly lost it. 
 "Life is the tragedy,' she said bitterly. 'You know how they categorize Shakespeare's plays, right? If it ends with a wedding, it's a comedy. And if it ends with a funeral, it's a tragedy. So we're all living tragedies, because we all end the same way, and it isn't with a goddamn wedding." 
 -- Robyn Schneider, The Beginning of Everything 
 From beginning to end I was completely sucked into the book and Ezra's thoughts. I feel like if there's an adult out there who understands what it's like to be a teenager this day and age it's Robyn Schneider. I said before in this review that reading this book in itself felt like a privilege, and I still think that. I think through Ezra, Robyn perfectly captured the funny/angst/scariness of being a teen. And through Ezra, Cassidy and Toby, Robyn captured parts of herself. She gave us readers a brief glimpse of what it's like to be inside her head. And for that I feel privileged. All I ask now is that Robyn Schneider NEVER stop writing.

Whimsically fun, but there's far more spoof than substance here--which was likely the intent in the first place. As a spoof, it works rather well. The sci-fi world owes an immeasurable debt to the Star Trek television franchise, and this entire novel is a gentle ribbing at the shortcomings of the series (like why the bridge always has to explode in sparks during battle scenes when it's the farthest point from the actual damage). As a novel, though, it felt far too self-aware for me to lose myself in the story, with enough winks and nods interspersed throughout the story to continually remind the reader that this is all a lark. 
 What threw me for a loop is that the codas made a sudden transition to seriousness, and I wasn't sure what to do with it.  That divergence also made the novel seem much less cohesive, as though too many things were being attempted without enough narrative glue to hold it together. Everything works independently, but packaging the material in one novel seems forced and even a bit contrived. The incessant use of "he said" also started to drive me batty, especially in lengthy scenes of back-and-forth dialogue where those words closed every single line of speech. It made the whole experience feel more like a rough draft rather than a final copy.
