Read: January 2016 
 Bookmarks: 4.5 
 I am not a novella kind-a girl. To me, they are just a money grubbing scheme to get more money by flogging a dead horse. They do not appeal to me, even in series I like. However, I did purchase Assassin's Blade as a bundle deal purchase and well....damn 
 Assassin's Blade is composed of 5 novella's that blend so beautifully together that is does read like a novel. That in itself made me impressed. You want to know what else impressed me. It focused on Celaena and how she came to be when we first meet her in Throne of Glass, all the while not spoiling Throne of Glass or any of the other books. Now, let me say this now, I read this before reading Throne of Glass, so I had little to no knowledge of what the hell was happening apart from awesome assassin kicking some ass. 
 I am going to review each novella on its own merit. 
 The Assassin and the Pirate Lord: 5 bookmarks 
 It took me awhile to get into the swing of things, but like beginning with any new novel where the characters are all new to you, that was expected. When I finally fell into my groove, I was grinning from ear to ear as I took in every word. 
 I went in expecting some cold heartless assassin and Celaena is like that but with this novella you see there is a person within that killing machine exterior. I liked that- I LOVED that. It made Celaena complex, made her more real and by far a more interesting character. Sure, seeing her killing and doing what she has been trained to do is awesome, but if she didn't have some form of compassion she would fail as a character. 
 The Assassin and the Healer: 4.5 bookmarks 
 This story is the result of her actions in The Assassin and the Pirate Lord. In traveling to the Silent Assassin's, she encounters a young barmaid and helps her in her time of need. The only reason I gave this 4.5 bookmarks isn't because it was written any less beautifully, or that Celaena's character had dramatically change. To me, the story didn't fit in. I know it is there so when a time comes in the series and we see the barmaid again, which I am assuming will happen, we will know her and Celaena's backstory. But it was a bit long for something that really didn't move the story forward. 
 The Assassin and the Desert: 5 bookmarks 
 ASSASSIN'S!!!! So many assassin's in one place and nothing happens! Haha So if nothing happens, why in the hell did I give it 5 bookmarks? Because there is SO much character development. Celaena makes her first, true friend...ever. To me that was a MAJOR growth for her character. She opened up to her and was quickly reminded why she never does. This story resounded with me, I think about it constantly. So much happens that shapes Celaena and I love it. 
 The Assassin and the Underworld: 5 bookmarks 
 We are finally given what we came for. Celaena assassinating people! We she her at a vulnerable stage where she realizes that she isn't invincible. I liked this story, I really did. Again, you get a new look at Celaena, dig deeper into the complexity of her character. 
 The Assassin and the Empire: 5 bookmarks and a vile of my tears as an offering 
 I'm not even...I can't. 
 My heart has been torn out, smashed into pieces before my eyes punted across the room. The only other time I have ever-EVER cried whist reading was Deathly Hallows when Fred died, and then again when Snape died. Congratulations Sarah J. Maas, you have made the teeny tiny list of authors who have made me tear up and sob like a child. Well done you, not sure if I hate you or admire you. Characters that I knew so little about, was still becoming invested in held that impact on me. 
 Sarah J. Mass all I want to say is, you have quickly become a favourite author of mine...

This is the second in the Armand Gamache series, and I think it's safe to say that I am hooked. I enjoy the omniscient third person point of view that is a little less jarring now that I am used to it, and you have to give credit to an author who can make living in Canada in the winter sound appealing. 
 Though I've rated it the same, I probably liked this installment slightly less than the first. It is difficult to wish to see a murder solved with quite the same intensity when the deceased is one that everyone hates and her murderer is obvious from the beginning. There was a slight swerve that almost threw me at the end, but not quite. 
 Like many other reviewers, I have to say that I was disappointed with the author's treatment of CC's depressed and verbally abused daughter, Cri. Penny does a wonderful job of creating varied characters, but the most negative feature she seems to be able to give someone is obesity. Poor 14 year old Cri is in turn teased and ignored simply because she is fat. We are told that she is intelligent and has a beautiful singing voice, but that simply cannot make up for the fact that she is not much (or perhaps too much) to look at. Even her teachers call her Brie. How cruel. 
 I enjoyed the description of the 'three Graces' and their life long relationship. Learning more about Clara's art and some hidden issues in Gamache's life was intriguing and encouraged me to carry on with the series. Three Pines may be the sort of place that can only exist in a novel, but it is pleasant to visit - except they have a Murder She Wrote propensity for unusual deaths. 
 What really keeps me reading this series is the quality of the writing. The descriptions of the town, the people, and the ability to peer into people's minds. I may not agree with the author's conclusions on some matters, but I cannot argue with how beautifully they are presented. 
 "I was tired of seeing the Graces always depicted as beautiful young things. I think wisdom comes with age and life and pain. And knowing what matters." 
 "In my teens my drug of choice was acceptance, in my twenties it was approval, in my thirties it was love, in my forties it was Scotch." 
 "Myrna looked out the window and wondered whether their peace, so fragile and precious, was about to be shattered. Since CC de Poitiers had arrived there'd been a gathering gloom over their little community. She'd brought something unsavory to Three Pines, in time for Christmas."
Well... It was okay, but not nearly as good as the originals. It was great to have the characters back, and there were some funny quips here and there, but the plot was not that interesting.

Life of Pi by Yann Martel (2001) 
 I can see why there is such a range in opinions regarding this book. Reading others' reviews, I see how much some people despise it while others are completely moved by it. I fall into the latter group - for me, something resonated deeply. 
 I could probably spend 227 days replying to other people's reviews, especially those that didn't enjoy it; but I think what it comes down to is that you have to read this book as a philosophical, spiritual, and/or religious journey. It IS about religion; or perhaps, more accurately, God. It says so in the Author's Note "Then the elderly man said, 'I have a story that will make you believe in God.'" 
 So, if you are not prepared to examine this story as an allegory from that perspective, then I suppose you won't really enjoy the book. If I was to speculate as to a couple of reasons why someone would NOT enjoy this book, I would say that Part 1 is slow-moving. There is a really BIG set-up in this book and the set-up is extremely important in understanding the rest of the book. In particular, descriptions of zoo life, including the temperament and care of the zoo animals is important; as is Pi's devotion to God and practice of three different religions (i.e., Hindu, Muslim, and Christianity). 
 For anyone thinking of reading this book or who has started and is having trouble moving forward...be patient. Every piece of information from these early chapters contributes to the understanding of Parts 2 and 3. If you are a person that likes to skip over parts, or likes to skip to the end, seriously...don't bother picking up this book. It's totally not for you. This book is about the journey. I've read reviews saying that Parts 1, 2 and 3 are disjointed - I couldn't disagree more; in fact, I would argue that they are three necessary parts to the whole. 
 Another reason I think some people would NOT like this book is the ambiguous ending. The story told in Part 2 is absolutely riveting. Martel is a brilliant story-teller. I could envision myself in Pi's shoes and followed with the ups and downs in his psyche as he experienced them being shipwrecked. It would have been a really great story if the end had been Pi's (and Richard Parker's) rescue. In fact, I bet that for those that didn't like the book, they would have given a higher rating if it had ended like that. (Just guessing). But, instead Martel offers an alternative account of Pi's experience (stripped down and much more horrific). The ending thus can leave the reader puzzled, frustrated, or perhaps even angry (based on reading others' reviews). 
 Most people tend to like nice tight and neat endings after investing so much time, emotion, and energy to reading a book. Martel's story leaves us hanging and allows the reader to choose the ending they believe. I still get goosebumps reading the text that brings it all together (from Chapter 99, p. 317): 
 "'So tell me, since it makes no factual difference to you and you can't prove the question either way, which story do you prefer? Which is the better story, the story with animals or the story without animals?' Mr. Okamoto: 'That's an interesting question?' Mr. Chiba: 'The story with animals.' Mr. Okamoto: 'Yes. The story with animals is the better story.' Pi Patel: 'Thank you. And so it goes with God.'" 
 Brilliant!! This is the text that brings together all three parts of the book. I love the way a few little sentences can pull together a whole story. Love it! This passage brings to mind the stories from the Old Testament, Daniel and the Lion's Den, Noah's Ark, the Tower of Babel, etc. Those were some good stories, weren't they?  
 Ok, so at the end of the day, Martel's writing is superb, the story is absolutely riveting, and the ending is thought-provoking. I can see myself reading this book in a few years with a fresh perspective and re-interpreting the story. It is THAT kind of book.

Where STRINGS was over-the-top cray-cray, showing us a glimpse of the world of rock and roll, BEATS is a quieter, darker salute to the messiness of love and relationships. 
 Jinx is a chameleon--putting on a different face for everyone she comes into contact with, but without knowing who she is without those external cues. And she's in love with Toombs, who's in love with and in an unofficial D/s relationship with their male bandmate, Rax. Toombs and Rax do everything together, and Toombs does what Rax tells him to do. When Rax sets his sights on Jinx, he gives her the opportunity to be with Toombs...so long as she understands she'd be with Rax, too. She can't pass up the opportunity for one night with Toombs, and agrees, despite sweating bullets over the prospect. Good Catholic girls don't have threesomes, right? 
 Jinx's stress isn't just unrequited love. She feels responsible for her family, who are still at home and struggling financially. She has a younger brother who has special needs. She has to put together the beats for Killer Buzz Float's upcoming album--and has lost her creative spark. 
 Letty (from STRINGS--if you haven't read it yet, stop reading this review and go get it!) is her normal, adorably crazy self, and offers some comedic relief for a story that could easily get bogged down with serious matters. 
 This story will resonate with anyone having financial stress, feeling responsible for others, or wanting to be with someone who (at least on the surface) seems unattainable. Provided, of course, you can also handle HOT, RAUNCHY, and EXPLICIT SEX! Please heed the warning at the beginning of the blurb. If you don't like explicit erotic scenes, this is NOT the book for you.

When I read Shades of Milk and Honey, I wasn't that impressed -- even when I reread it. But I quite liked Glamour in Glass. Probably partly out of sheer bloodymindedness; I looked at some reviews and oh how they whined about Jane's attitude to pregnancy in this book. And I thought, wait: that's actually interesting. Yes, let's address how dangerous pregnancy could be at that time. Let's address how "confinement" literally imprisoned women. Yes! Let's discuss the aftermath of the Austen and Heyer novels and their neat marriages: the babies, the risks to the women, how those women were limited. 
 Someone called it anti-pregnancy, and I don't think it's that. It just turns to something that went unspoken in that period, and scrutinises it a little, and articulates a fear and dread of the constraints pregnancy placed upon women (shown even more clearly in this world because a woman can't work any glamour while pregnant). It's still a fairly light read, despite that theme; I read it in an hour and a half, so if you're a fan of the first book, don't think that it's suddenly changed entirely in style and subject. 
 This is less frothy than the first book, seriously examining the relationship between Vincent and Jane, their equality and finding a balance between them. I anticipated the political plot ahead of time (perhaps because I'm fresh from Voyage of the Basilisk); it feels a bit rushed, honestly, particularly toward the end, but I appreciated seeing Jane and Vincent facing down these issues, and his growing regard for and trust in her.

This book. Gaah.

 Lachlan Crow is a potential heir to the throne of the Irish mafia in Boston. He's described as quiet and reserved, but make no mistake-he's calculating, menacing...definitely not a man to be fucked with. After the recent untimely death of his grand-da, he's out for revenge, but it must be done delicately and diplomatically, so as not to soil a pending alliance with the Russians. 
 Okay I admit I'm on a Peaky Blinders kick right now, shutup. 
 Mackenzie "Mack" Wilder is a tough girl from Southie with a dark past and a single mission on her mind: to find her best friend, Talia, who has been missing for almost a year. Mack knows that nothing good can possibly have befallen her troubled friend, who was last seen working a new job at Slainte, a bar/strip club and front for the Irish mafia. Finding the Feds incredibly unhelpful and apathetic to her cause, she boldly decides to take on her own undercover mission. 
 Mack's method of making herself known and remembered in front of the Irish is bold and borderline insane. And it works. She immediately catches the attention of Lachlan and from there, there's no shaking it. Not that she wants to. A man in his position possesses peak potential for gathering the information she needs. Doesn't hurt that he's a sexy Irish mob boss with tats, abs, and a penchant for boxing. Did I mention the dirty talk? 
 What I really love about this book is the alternating narrative. On Mack's end, we see the internal struggle she has as she battles a deep-seeded guilt for not protecting her friend in her time of need, and subsequently "sleeping with the enemy" (as she sees it). As her feelings continue to grow for Lachlan, it becomes increasingly problematic and at odds with her mission to spy on him and uncover more information. 
 On Lachlan's end, we get to see a similar internal battle. His job comes with several obligations that make his obsession with Mack a dangerous distraction that puts them both at risk. 
 Suffice it to say, any book I read that I must finish in one sitting gets an automatic five stars. Really looking forward to the next one, Reaper, which is apparently all about Ronan! I'm stoked. I have so many questions about this character.

 Claire is on her fourth fiance when her "curse" strikes again but Lord Alexander Pembrooke miraculously shows up and wants to be her fifth. 
 Years of planning have finally put Alex in position to destroy his old friend Lord Paul, gaining the beautiful Claire is simply a bonus. 
 Old hurts and lies by omission will work to keep Alex and Claire apart if they can't figure out how to open their hearts to one another. 
 "Our marriage is based upon hate and revenge." 
 First in the Cavensham Heiresses series, The Bad Luck Bride is Janna MacGregor's debut book. The prologue was intense, dark, and intriguing as we get introduced to our hero Alexander and his two friends, Lord Somerton and Lord Paul. There's betrayal, pain, anger, and hurt, all set in a swirling snow storm; I was instantly hooked. As the story went on though, the author had a tendency to overwrite (a bit too descriptive at times for my tastes), the cast of characters became a bit overwhelming, the story started to drag with repetitiveness, and the focus on the lead's chemistry faded away. 
 Alex misinterpreted a suicide note left by his sister and blamed his friend Lord Paul for her death. This is the catalyst for the story as he works to destroy Paul and leads Alex to marrying Claire. If we would have just had this one misunderstanding, I would have went with it but Alex is a rush to judgment guy and the repeating of him getting angry and then saying oops (not the best apology man) was a bit frustrating. 
 I liked Claire in the beginning as she seemed unfairly saddled with the "curse" talk but we lose her as the story goes on. The curse was brought up so much, I almost thought I was reading a medieval and it was a big deal because people wanted to burn the witch at the stake. I wish it would have been handled more as a bullying tactic the ton was using instead of the awkward heavier weight it was given, especially since it isn't fully explained until the very end. 
 When our leads first meet, I loved the chemistry they had, their discourse had some great by-play but as the story went on, due to the overload of the curse talk, overly handful of secondary characters, and forced angst, Alex and Claire seemed to be kept apart more than they were together. Their fights and flushing out of feelings was less interactions and more in their own heads, I prefer the characters to interact more. 
 I wish the editor had been heavier handed as trimming up side tangents that become repetitive or simply didn't add much to the story, could have made this stronger as more scenes and the focus would have been more on what worked, the chemistry between the leads. There's also some series baiting characters, I'll be interested to see if the author plans on trying to redeem Lord Paul as he seems to have gotten a raw deal but also had a tendency to tell some lies that make him pretty hard to like. 
 As a debut though, I can see the hints of promise this author has and will be interested in trying her again.

The Dinner by Herman Koch turned out to be a book that I would never ever read again or recommend to anyone to waste their time reading. To summarize, two couples are meeting for dinner to discuss what to do about the terrible thing that their teenagers did and somehow was caught on video. Opposite ends of the parental spectrum, one wants them to confess while the other will stop at nothing to keep it secret. All of this plays out over the course of the worst dinner ever. 
 I get that the author was trying to show the complexity of family interactions and how we really don't know what we would do until faced with a no win situation. However, the characters behave in such odd ways, were terribly unlikable and although I can understand the writers purpose, I just can't get around the convenience of the plot. With the single point of view the narrator, we are only able to experience all these moving parts from his perspective only. Combined with odd flashbacks and the ending seems as if the writer was trying to prove a point but forgot to let the reader know. 
 Overall, I'd give it a D.

 Spin-Off of characters in the Hitched trilogy (Sterling Quinn and Camryn Palmer) 
 Sterling has to be married in 6 months to get his inheritance of 50-Million+ from his grandfather, according to his grandfather's will. Apparently, his grandpa decided it was time for playboy Sterling to settle down. Sterling's Uncle Charlie hires publicist Camryn Palmer from Olivia's publicity firm - Olivia of Noah and Olivia from the "Hitched" trilogy. Sterling's always thought he could have a "thing" for Camryn, but his playboy ways kept him from asking her out - she wants something too serious, he thinks. Camryn's had a crush on Sterling forever, but as usual, she's been waiting for Sterling to make the first move. 
 OK, here's the thing: This author has a penchant for "forcing" people into relationships by wills or trusts or whatever. It's hokey. And the fact that neither Sterling nor Camryn seriously considers getting married or even dating with the idea of fulfilling the 6 month term/marriage is beyond me. Everyone acts as if the will specifically says that Sterling *can't* date or marry Camryn or anyone working for him - so untrue. It's so OBVIOUS, people! We all know where this is going... and we could still have a story without some of this... this... stuff! 
 So why did I read the book? Good question. The truth is, despite some of the outlandish suspension of disbelief, there's something about these stories that sucks me in - the covers? (Hot!) The alpha arrogant male POV? (Maybe). The writing is decent - no annoying typos, glaring mistakes, eye-rolling euphemisms, or troublesome e-book formatting. 
 I guess that these books are just plain fluff and steam for me - a guilty pleasure that fills a quick craving.

I liked her character from the beginning which is unusual for me, I usually find them annoying at first. I think it was partly because she's a part of Amnesty International. I'm more of a Greenpeace girl myself. Saving sharks from becoming tuna and all that jazz. 
 I actually liked the love interest! A certain blogger will love me for this. Usually I'm quite picky but Nick was a really good character and actually fit in with the story instead of just being there or having the story centred around him. I liked that his and Zara's relationship was there but not really full on and heavy like in other books. Usually I feel like I'm suffocating with it. 
 When you start the book it might feel a little like Twilight but I didn't notice that until a review pointed it out. Sure, Zara's mom has packed her off to a small town but I honestly didn't notice any Twilight references as the plot is a lot stronger and the characters aren't cardboard.

 There's a few cliched moments in this and moments where you go 'I knew it!' but that's to be expected after all. I'm curious to see how the plot develops in the next book as this could quite easily have been a stand-alone.

I have probably read, and reread this book at least 4 or 5 times. Each time, I fall more and more in love with it's characters and the story. This book was release in audiobook format on 7/22/13, so I took advantage of that, and bought it so that I could read it yet again. This book transitioned into audio form very well. The story itself is a wonderfully unique paranormal tale, where the heroine faces challenges and situations where she is faced with tough decisions that can affect not only her life, but the lives of the ones she holds dear. The story is told from Evie's POV, and I found that I truly enjoyed seeing the world in her eyes. At times I've found that when reading YA books such as this, the heroine at times can become frustrating, whiny, annoying, or even boring, but that is not the case with Evie. I felt that she was genuine, intriguing, and just REAL. Another thing that I loved about this story, was that all of the characters, big and small, played a role and contributed something interesting. I loved all of the characters (good and bad). Each added their own dynamic that only enhanced the reading experience. 
 Now, to discuss the aspects of the audio book: the narrator was EXCELLENT. I loved how well she was able to perform the story without it coming across cheesy or uninteresting. Sometimes with a female narrator, male voices can be overdone, and it tends to ruin a book for me. This narrator did a great job with Reed and Russell's voices. My only gripe that I had was that her interpretation of Zepher wasn't what I personally pictured when I first read his character in the book. But that's only one minor problem in what was practically a flawless audio production. 
 If you're a love of paranormal YA, you need to read this book. Whether you download it to Kindle, purchase in paperback, or get it in audio, you won't be disappointed. Brace yourself for awesomeness! :)

Spoilers ahead! Do not read if you haven't read Shiver and Linger. 
 This book. This book was very emotional in my opinion. Especially when it came to Cole and Grace as individuals. They both were going through the first crucial part of the shifting process, and it was hard to get through. In my eyes, I found it hard to read without cringing. It was that emotional. Maybe it's because I've stuck to this series since Shiver came out, and I've gotten that into it. I don't know. But that's how it was. 
 It was fascinating to watch Grace transform from a innocent, love ridden girl, to a new kind of species on her behalf. She seemed stronger than before. Still a bit stubborn, but strong. Confident even. I loved that part about her. Despite the pain on her part, I think becoming a wolf was best for her. 
 Sam and Grace is an example of true love, from day 1, he loved her when she was attacked by those wolves. You could tell it. They stuck by each other through all of this. It's a different kind of love. But you can sense the ferocity of it. 
 I loved how Maggie ended the series. It wasn't quite a cliffhanger, but it left you guessing, "What happens to Sam and Grace now that they're both wolves?" or, "What happens to Cole and Isabel relationship? Will it blossom into something?" And among other questions that would give away too much. ;) 
 Cole has to be my favorite character. Not because he seems like the bad-boy type. But because of what he's been through. He's a tormented person trying to set himself free. Which is quite literal in a sense. I feel for him, I really do. Plus Isabel just needs to loosen up and give into him. Seriously lol. 
 This is the last book of the series, and it's a damn good and painful way to end it. I approve. 
 Now. Time to go to bed and cry myself to sleep and be depressed.

"If you don't start with crazy, crazy love, the kind of love that Van Morrison sings about, then you don't have a shot to go the distance. Love's a marathon, not a sprint." 
 Ahh, what a romantic, lovely sentiment. Worthy of a daily mantra or a morning affirmation to keep love fresh and alive in one's heart 
 But...as you could imagine, these words take on an entirely different tone depending on the speaker. You's main character: Joe is an interesting lad. Dark, obsessive, and disturbed, but interesting nonetheless. He has found his one true love and has totally fixated on her, and he'll be damned if he lets anything (or anyone) stand in his way. The entire book is exclusively in his perspective. Every thought, every feeling, every interaction...and it all circles back to her. 
 I LOVED You! Reading the perspective of a stalker will likely not be everyone's cup of tea, but Ms. Kepnes' writing style definitely appeals to the masses. Joe's character is so intelligently crafted. The writing adds plenty of humor and smile-worthy moments to lighten up the dark themes and the insightful POV allows the reader to connect the dots between Joe's thought process and actions. Joe has surprisingly become one of my all-time favorite characters (in terms of fascination) and You will without a doubt be a re-read for me very soon. 
 My favorite quote: 
 "What a shame to be so angered by what you don't have that you treat what you do have like it's nothing."

If only tears could talk, they would tell you how much I loved this story.. 
 They would tell you that pages can radiate emotions, that words can create feelings, that beauty can hurt. 
 If tears could talk.. they would tell you how they dropped on this book drowning smiles in emotions, drowning sadness and turning it into in happiness, making me heart melt slowly and leaving me with a sweet taste of hope. 
 "You're an angel among mortals. Echos are asked to sacrifice everything to make another family, other people, happy. To give them hope. You are hope." 
 Sometimes I read sad books that make me happy... How ironic, huh? 
 But it's true.. I love reading stories about humans, about the human nature in fact, about their essence, about their deep, raw feelings. Figuratively, I love the sound of my heart breaking with every word, with every new nuance discovered.. There's a beauty that can't be put into words, it hurts but it also makes me feel complete, because books like this one are everything I want and then a whole lot more. 
 I am at a loss for words, you know, and this only happens when I truly love a story. When it touches my heart, when it turns my life upside down, when it hurts to turn the last page and let go of a world so cruel but so beautiful, of these characters so perfect in their flaws. 
 I loved every bit of it and I can't get tired of telling you how amazingly beautiful this book really was for me. 
 It's like a part of me on paper, as someone said: if I were to write a book, this would be it. If I were to be a character, I would be named after a stubborn elephant in a zoo, I would feel trapped in a crazy world but I would grow wings and make myself fly. I would love with all my heart and I would always hope to find my way back home. I would fight, I would survive, I would believe in myself even when no one else will. I would play nice but I would never forget who I am, I would never stop trying to find my way to freedom. 
 "But maybe that's what the dead do. They stay. They linger. Benign and sweet and painful. They don't need us. They echo all by themselves." 
 The story: 
 I've always asked myself: what are we without our choices, without the will to live our own lives by our rules and desires, without the will to be ourselves? 
 When you look in a mirror, what do you see? 
 What are you without that part that can't be seen: the inner you, the real you.. Can you be someone else, can you leave your own self behind and be that mirror? 
 Can you bury your feelings, fake your thoughts, be a puppet in a world that doesn't want you but uses you for what you represent, for the image you mirror? 
 ...And here goes question after question and the truth is that this is just a tiny piece of what this story might be about. 
 The Love: 
 I loved the relationship between Eva and Shaun - their friendship was strong, their love was so sweet and innocent. They matched like no others, perfect in every way. 
 I loved how he saw her as a real human, I loved that he believed in her without any doubt, that he was there for her when she needed him the most, that he loved her and he never thought that she was just a reflection in a mirror, but a girl that deserves to be loved, to be cherished, to be given a second chance. Their romance was sweet, their connection strong, their chemistry palpable.. you could feel it in their little conversations, in their little fights, in their desires, their hopes for the other's safety and freedom. They melted my heart like no other couple, and if there is another book to follow (like a second book in a series) I hope to see more of them, together. 
 "You," he says, before the door closes all the way. "I often dream of you." 
 The Family: 
 I loved the connection between Eva and the 'familiars'. 
 How the supposed brother saw her as herself not a copy and he wanted to protect her, and how the little sister Amarra left behind was so sweet and innocent. How the mother wanted to see her daughter still in Eva and how the father never got over his grief and couldn't make himself believe in a fantasy. 
 Also, I liked the guardians that represented Eva's real family - or the only one she ever had. How they loved her and wanted to keep her safe in their way. How they treated her like a person and wanted her to acknowledge that as well. 
 The Friendship: 
 I could understand Amarra's friends, how they wanted her back, how they felt betrayed, how they all loved her, but I was happy to see Eva make new friends, create her own path. She tried a lot to be the best version of Amarra, but at the end she felt the need to be herself again, to take a break from that all, to just.. be. 
 "She was right. I am the thief. I've taken everything that belongs to her. She's had to give it all up. What must that be like, to know that every single thing you wear, every last thing you know, is being copied, mimicked, duplicated halfway across the world 
 I feel the need to talk a bit about Ray too (the boy Eva never did study what was like to kiss, as the synopsis says). I didn't understand how he got away with the accident, but I did care about him. I felt his pain, his hope, his struggle when things didn't add up. It saddened me to see how much he wished for Eva to really be Amarra. 
 ...But there were times when I wanted to punch him right in the face too. 
 The Pain and grief: 
 Here goes the family next to Ray. 
 They were all so different and they saw her in such a different light. 
 I felt their love for Amarra, I saw them caring more and more for Eva, I felt their inner struggle, the fight between what is right and what is wrong, between their desire and their reasoning.. it was really heartbreaking. 
 Tiny, tiny little bug: 
 The IT girl in me kept screaming: a few hundreds years later (I can only assume) and they still use CDs (aka. the disks)? Come on, we barely use them anymore, if they can "stitch" life they must do better than that o_O 
 CONCLUSION: 
 What an awesome, awesome read! 
 It cut my heart right open and I loved it from the first page to the last one, and its echo still lingers here.. 
 Happy midnight reading!

 I've been rushing to read as many 2016 Printz contenders as I can before the awards are announced, but since I finished The Walls Around Us two days ago, I haven't wanted to pick up a new book. I didn't have this experience with Bone Gap, which I read right before this and is, from what I'm seeing online, most people's pick for the win. I liked Bone Gap, but I loved The Walls Around Us. 
 This novel is narrated by two girls, Amber (incarcerated in Aurora Hills Juvenile Detention Center) and Violet (about to leave home to attend Julliard in New York City). They are connected by Orianna, Violet's former best friend, who is now locked up with Amber at Aurora Hills for violently murdering two fellow ballerinas. Violet tells the story of her friendship with Orianna, ending with the incident that resulted in Orianna's arrest, and Amber describes life at Aurora Hills from the inside. Typically when I read a book with more than one POV, I find myself looking forward to one narrator's chapters over another, but that wasn't the case here. Both narrators have compelling stories to tell. As Violet's story unfolded I found myself wanting to fling the book away - she is that creepy. And Amber functions as the voice for all of the prisoners at Aurora Hills, often using second person plural to explain what it's like to be one of its forty-two residents: 
 Some of us knew for sure it was a Saturday, the first one of August. Some of us kept track of days... Then there were those of us who didn't want to keep track, whose sentences ran as long as a set of train tracks to all the places we'd never been. We pretended weeks were days, and years were weeks. That we still got to live our lives out in the sunshine. 
 In a way, The Walls Around Us reminded me of a Gillian Flynn novel, in that it has a female character so depraved, so completely off-the-charts insane, that I was chilled to the bone. It's the kind of story that makes you wary of everyone around you, even - especially - your closest friends. This book is, as so many reviewers have said before me, extremely disturbing. It's also the best YA novel I've read this year. Beautifully written, as I'm finding is typical for Nova Ren Suma, but also very controlled. The paranormal elements are handled well and the ending, while a little crazy, is satisfying. The Walls Around Us gripped me much harder than Bone Gap did, and overall, I think this book just worked better. Its voice was stronger. I don't think it's likely to win the Printz award over Bone Gap or Challenger Deep, but I hope it gets an honor. It has my vote, anyway. 
 Home is where the heart is, and where the hell is, and where the hopelessness is. Which made Aurora Hills pretty much like home.

** spoiler alert ** 
 "Was it really some other person I was so anxious to discover, when I did all of that looking, or was it only my own solitude that I could not abide?" 
 Wittgenstein's Mistress is about a woman who may or may not be the last woman on earth - who may or may not have traveled across Eastern and Western Europe, the United States and Mexico. She may or may not have had a husband named Adam and a son named Simon. She may or may not have seen a cat in the Colliseum in Rome. She may or may not have survived by building fires and living in large, famous museums all over the world. Alone. 
 I liked this mostly for the idea of it. It's stream of consciousness wandering and references to art, history and literature can be challenging. Given the nature and style of the book, it's no wonder that it encountered 54 rejections before finally getting published. Mel recommended it to me because I liked the style of Wittgenstein's Tractatus - and the style, though not overtly similar, has a consonant feel. A narrative of trying to organize and defend one's thoughts against chaos. 
 In the Afterword, Wittgenstein's Mistress is described as the best illustration of Wittgenstein's proposition that "philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language." Throughout Kate's stream of consciousness rambling, she makes connections weaving together paintings, classic epic poems, buildings and the like - any or all of which might be incorrect and mis-remembered, and she struggles with this through the entire narrative. She frequently loses track of things she wanted to remember, and then picks up the thread later to almost comic relief. 
 For those who value such facts, Wittgenstein is most frequently mentioned (after the two quotes at the beginning) in Kate's narrative in reference to his interactions with Bertrand Russell, to whether or not Wittgenstein played an instrument and which one, and to the fact that (Kate believes she read) the Wittgenstein never read a word of Aristotle. 
 UPDATE: Okay, I just had to add one more quote that I love, and then really I'm through with this review. Really. 
 Surely if Wittgenstein was as intelligent as one was generally led to believe he ought to have been able to tell me if that had meant anything, either. 
 Then again, something else I once read about Wittgenstein was that he used to think so hard that you could actually see him doing it. 
 And certainly I would have had no desire to put the man to that sort of trouble. 
 Wasn't that worth the update? 
 I thought so too. 
 I also upgraded this book from three stars to four. 
 By tomorrow, when I've had a full night to think on it, I may upgrade it too five. 
 UPDATE No. 2: Really, this is the very last quote I'm going to include, but I just had to include it. 
 "Men are so necessarily mad, that not to be mad would amount to another form of madness, which happens to be one more sentence that I now remember I once underlined." 
 I love that line. Just another example of the sort of narrative structure that you will either love or really hate. Yes, it's about 240 pages of that exact kind of thing. Maybe it's just that my 'inner voice' (especially when I haven't had any sleep) sounds so very much like that. Which is comforting on one hand (in that, 'oh look, I'm not the only one who thinks like that sometimes') and a bit alarming on the other hand (in the, 'oh great I must be daft then, too') sort of way. 
 What the hell, why wait til morning. Five stars it is!

 As a side note, this book taught me that all you need to get a 700k dolars deal are cupcakes, so I may start baking right about now. 
 The veredict 
 The only way I could recommend this is if you want to;

 4 stars! Melted my heart! 
 This is such a highly compulsive read. I fell IN LOVE with the characters that Stephanie Perkins created with Lola and the Boy Next Door. Truthfully, this is a light and fun book. It will never be a literary classic so if that's what you're looking for, go elsewhere. But if you want something that is warm-hearted, deliciously unputdownable and just plain old high school crushin' fun? I'd check this little gem out. 
 Lola is the girl who stands out in a crowd, literally. She dresses eccentrically and makes no apologies for her love of costume. Her life is very well on it's way to being perfect. If only she could get her dads to approve of her sex god rocker boyfriend, Max. Life, however, has it's own plans for Lola when the infamous Bell twins move back in next door to her. Lola thought she was long over her days of pining over Cricket Bell. His re-emergence into her life now has her in a tailspin. What will Lola do about this unexpected turn in her story? 
 I think this book stuck out to me more than Anna and the French Kiss because I genuinely connected with Lola more than I did with Anna. I've seen the negative reviews stating her as absurd, not-realistic, too wacky, selfish and what have you. And while I saw those things as well, I also remembered being self-centered and melodramatic at 17 and still sometimes find myself as such at 23. I remember doing outlandish things to set myself apart from the crowd. I adore Lola because of her flaws. And like Lola, I make no apologies for it. 
 And I will say it openly, I am in love with a fictional 18 year old named Cricket Bell! So sue me. He is so damn likeable and so damn cute and awkward and GAHHHHHHH!!!! 
 My only criticisms for this book are as follows: 
 (1) The names are ridiculous. I found it endearing but I can see how that could throw someone off. 
 (2) Why'd you have to make Max a douche? I was already rooting for Cricket. Yeah, I want for there to be tension. But I want to feel like its a struggle to choose between two love interests. I did feel like some of it was believable but some parts were just not. And that didn't work for me. Which is what held this book back from being a 4.5 or 5 star rating.  
 However, those were minor points in the grand scheme. The truth is that I tore through this book. Now I'm genuinely distraught that I'll never read this book for the first time ever again. I don't know what to do with my life. 
 If you don't mind, I'm going to weep into my raw cookie dough and long to live in San Fran with these ridiculously-named, lovable hooligans.

 Maas's "A Court of Thorns and Roses" is at its best mediocre. It will make you mad- very mad- but ultimately it is worth reading. The second ACOTAR book is 500% better, and I give you my word. Despite how little I enjoyed the first book, I'm really impressed by Maas's character development ability and how much she grows as a writer from book to book. She understands that women aren't perfect, so it's impossible to write perfect women. That's not to say that our hero Feyre is dumb and helpless, it's to say that she's human. In ACOTAR #2, A Court of Mist and Fury, Feyre realizes her strength and how she held herself back and how she let others hold her back. This is a very human crisis that Maas writes beautifully. Plus, if you think Tamlin is dreamy in ACOTAR, just WAIT until Rhysand in ACOMAF... Dear Lord. 
 Good things about ACOTAR #1: 
 Great world building. Maas is very, very skilled at world building without describing every tiny detail, sort of like Tolkien. ACOTAR is sort of like "Prithian: A History" and that's all that's really important about it. Like the Silmarillion but sexier. 
 Characterization is outstanding. It's very rare that I grow attached to characters in just one book, but Maas has a talent for making characters you absolutely love and absolutely hate. In ACOTAR #1, her strongest characters in terms of development and depth are Feyre, Tamlin, and Lucien. The ending is weak, so her weakest characters in ACOTAR are Amarantha and, ironically, Rhysand. 
 Sorta Poor Qualities of ACOTAR #1: 
 Not much action, just world building essentially and sexual tension. The main focus is on Feyre and Tamlin, so the rest of the story is pretty weak and underdeveloped. But boy, oh boy, does that change in ACOMAF. Please read ACOMAF. 
 Only lovable character is Feyre, which can turn off readers and not make them want to read the next book. BUT PLEASE, I BEG YOU, READ ACOMAF. You will fall in love with like seven faeries I promise. 
 Another big thing that bothers me, especially in YA fantasy, is that most characters are white and straight. This may not seem like a big deal to some, but for many it is, especially if you're not actually white and straight. It's 2017. YA writers (and they're mostly white) need to realize this. 
 It's overall just kinda a weak book. Weak beginning, weak rising action (if there really is any... Things just kinda... Happen.) and weak ending, although the ending is the strongest out of the book. Maas does a good job of setting up the next book subtly, but it's still weak and doesn't really leave you craving the next book... I only read ACOMAF because my friend begged me to and because I'd spoiled a bit of it for myself on Tumblr... So don't go on Tumblr before you read ACOMAF because those suckers will RUIN the book for you because ACOMAF is so dang good!!!! 
 *** 
 So I hoped this helped you decide whether or not to read ACOTAR #1... I was really skeptical at first because I really, really hate YA fiction... Before ACOTAR the last YA novel I'd read was "The Winner's Curse," and wow what kinda racist trash. I was appalled. And although ACOTAR's characters are pretty much all white and all straight, it avoids cliches and is kinda a breath of fresh air. But again, it's ACOMAF that really got me.
There's absolutely nothing wrong with this book - I suspect it is a very good book. It's just not the book I want to read right now.

My expectations for this book weren't all that high. I read the Hex Hall series years ago and those, while very enjoyable, didn't blow me away. Rebel Belle was really great, but its sequels... were not. Half way through, I though this would end up a 4 star read like the series it spun off from. Fun, but not much more. 
 Listening to the end, though, I realised how much I actually loved this book. It was more than just fun (though it certainly was that), it was gripping and well thought out and I was very much emotionally invested. After some of my recent listens (Champion series, Empire of Storms, even the last few Vampire Academy books), I though maybe romances just didn't work as well on audiobook, but no. I really liked Izzy and Dex. And I absolutely love the friendship between Izzy and Romy. It just seemed so normal. Aside from the ghost stuff, that is. Obviously. But seriously, that friendship was just really nice. No jealousy, no fighting over a guy, no competing. Just two girls being awesome and hanging out. 
 The end was strong both plot-wise and emotionally. I can see where the rest of the originally planned series would have gone, and while I would have loved to read that, I'm pretty happy with where we left everything. I can wrap it up pretty well in my head: They find the sister. Mirror guy maybe ends up being evil? NO LOVE TRIANGLE. Izzy and Dex get it on. They keep in touch with Romy and Anderson. Everyone lives happily ever after, still saving people and hunting things (the family business).  (Also, after what happened with Rebel Belle, maybe it's a good thing the rest was never written. Sorry...) 
 All together, this ended up being quite the hidden gem. So glad I finally picked it up. 
 ps You definitely don't need to read the Hex Hall books to understand this one, but School Spirits does spoil how some things end up in Spirit Bound, so if you want to read those, maybe do that first.
